Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) brought back Jensen Huang as president and CEO on Monday morning, 12 days after its board accepted his resignation, and the stock jumped 27% in pre-market trading to $159.48 as of 9 a.m. ET. Even at that price, Nvidia sits 33% below its record close of $239.24 on Oct. 6 and needs to rise another 50% to get back there. The board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang "effective immediately" as president, chief executive and a member of the board, the company said in a release at 8:55 a.m. ET. It said the vote followed "a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead NVIDIA." The release also said the board "received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk." President Trump had urged the board earlier Monday morning to rehire him. Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia's chair, said: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers." Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, keeps her job as chief financial officer, and Jones stays on as chair. Huang said: "I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution." He ended his statement: "I can't wait to get back to work." That is a turn from Nov. 17, when Jones said the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Nvidia closed at $173.73 on Nov. 11, the day the board accepted Huang's resignation, and fell 28% from there to $125.53 last Friday, capping its worst week since October 2008. This morning's price is still 8% below where the stock stood the day he left. Huang held about 811.5 million Nvidia shares as of his September filing, most of them through trusts and partnerships. At Friday's close those shares had lost about $92 billion of value since the Oct. 6 record. At $159.48, they have regained about $28 billion of it. The reinstatement does not end the investigation. The board said its committee of independent directors, formed after reports that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," will continue its work "to conclusion," and that Huang supports it and will cooperate. Nvidia also said it has formed a National Security and Export Control Committee made up of independent directors, and that it is searching for a new Chief Compliance Officer who will report to the board's nominating and governance committee. The company said it "will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries." extraction.body: Trump says he spoke to the board and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals . The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures. Huang had been seeking a return to Nvidia since shortly after his resignation, reportedly forming a war room to strategize how best to bring it to pass. Last week, Huang posted on social media that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” he wrote on Truth Social last week. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” In a social media post immediately following the reinstatement, Trump called it “the correct and proper decision” and confirmed that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” Appearing on CNBC Monday morning , Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that… he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents,” Trump said. “You have to protect our geniuses and there aren’t enough of them.” Huang’s tenure at Nvidia dates back to the company’s founding in 1993, when he and three cofounders were focused on the then-nascent field of GPU hardware aimed at PC gamers. In the decades since, the highly parallel cores in those GPUs have been embraced first by cryptocurrency miners and then AI companies, propelling the company to its position as the most valuable in the world at its October peak. Nvidia stock—the price of which had sunk roughly 25 percent since Huang’s resignation was announced and nearly 50 percent since its peak—was up about 30 percent in early morning trading in the immediate aftermath of Huang’s reinstatement announcement. Huang’s return in some ways echoes that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was fired almost exactly three years ago after the board said it “no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.” Two weeks later, Altman was back at the helm after many employees threatened a mass revolt and departure if he wasn’t brought back. In Huang’s case, the revolt following his departure came not from employees but from fellow titans of the tech industry. Executives including Altman, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey are among the prominent industry figures who have publicly offered him support in the days since his resignation. In its statement, the Nvidia board reiterated that it has retained independent counsel and formed a committee of independent directors to investigate what it calls Huang’s targeting by “a foreign intelligence effort.” The company has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and is seeking to hire a new chief compliance officer position. sources.title: Nvidia board puts Jensen Huang back as boss - The Register
passages: On the 11th day, Jensen Huang rose from the ranks of CEOs past and, with the full confidence of the board, returned to helm Nvidia

There's no telling what caused the Nvidia board to unanimously vote to reinstate Huang less than a week after saying his return wasn’t under consideration - except reportedly the threat of having one's head ripped off and brain peed on - but that really doesn't matter, at least as far as shareholders need to be concerned: Jensen's back in charge and all’s right in the world of chip stocks.
The White House has since confirmed that the senior-level official involved in Huang’s reinstatement was President Trump.
Nvidia stock has tumbled since Huang’s ouster, and much of the rest of the tech stock world followed suit .

Nvidia insiders and tech heavyweights have been pushing for Huang’s return for about as long as he was unemployed, but calls for his return from the US federal government may have been the catalyst for a change of heart among Nvidia leadership who didn’t want Huang back.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board chair Harvey Jones added.
Jones was made Nvidia's first board chair upon Huang’s resignation, and will remain in that role.
"The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security," Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." ®

extraction.body: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO. The company announced on Monday morning that the board “voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.” In its statement, the board says that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump responded to the board’s decision in a post on Truth Social, saying Nvidia “made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” The board’s statement says that its investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot will continue, with Huang’s support and cooperation, while interim CEO Colette Kress will continue as CFO, and Harvey Jones will remain as the recently appointed board chair. “I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process.” This move comes after Jones said during an earnings call last week that the Nvidia board “does not intend” to return Huang as CEO. Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month following reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including an executive who reported to him. In the wake of his departure, more than 200,000 people, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, signed a letter to Nvidia’s board, calling for his reinstatement. Nvidia shares tumbled in Huang’s absence, while industry analysts raised concerns about an outsider replacing him at a time when Nvidia is so critical to the AI boom. Nonetheless, the board maintained as recently as last Tuesday that Huang wasn’t coming back.

extraction.body: Trump says he spoke to the board and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals . The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures. Huang had been seeking a return to Nvidia since shortly after his resignation, reportedly forming a war room to strategize how best to bring it to pass. Last week, Huang posted on social media that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” he wrote on Truth Social last week. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” In a social media post immediately following the reinstatement, Trump called it “the correct and proper decision” and confirmed that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” Appearing on CNBC Monday morning , Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that… he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents,” Trump said. “You have to protect our geniuses and there aren’t enough of them.” Huang’s tenure at Nvidia dates back to the company’s founding in 1993, when he and three cofounders were focused on the then-nascent field of GPU hardware aimed at PC gamers. In the decades since, the highly parallel cores in those GPUs have been embraced first by cryptocurrency miners and then AI companies, propelling the company to its position as the most valuable in the world at its October peak. Nvidia stock—the price of which had sunk roughly 25 percent since Huang’s resignation was announced and nearly 50 percent since its peak—was up about 30 percent in early morning trading in the immediate aftermath of Huang’s reinstatement announcement. Huang’s return in some ways echoes that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was fired almost exactly three years ago after the board said it “no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.” Two weeks later, Altman was back at the helm after many employees threatened a mass revolt and departure if he wasn’t brought back. In Huang’s case, the revolt following his departure came not from employees but from fellow titans of the tech industry. Executives including Altman, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey are among the prominent industry figures who have publicly offered him support in the days since his resignation. In its statement, the Nvidia board reiterated that it has retained independent counsel and formed a committee of independent directors to investigate what it calls Huang’s targeting by “a foreign intelligence effort.” The company has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and is seeking to hire a new chief compliance officer position. The White House has since confirmed that the senior-level official involved in Huang’s reinstatement was President Trump.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board chair Harvey Jones added.

Recent outages affecting Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration and JPMorgan Chase have sparked anxiety as businesses accelerate software patching and upgrades to aging systems in an effort to prevent bad actors from exploiting software vulnerabilities with AI. CrowdStrike has been a major beneficiary of skyrocketing demand for AI security, with shares soaring about 80% this year as of Monday's open. Competitor Palo Alto Networks has also spent billions on several cyber and AI businesses, including startup Applied Compute and a $25 billion deal for CyberArk, which it closed earlier this year. Analysts view the Zscaler deal as a major AI security opportunity, allowing CrowdStrike to capture more customer security spending and close a significant gap with Palo Alto. "The addition of ZS to CRWD's platform could bring more breadth in an era of vendor consolidation and, more importantly, network security to position the company more effectively for rising demand for AI Sovereignty," wrote analysts at JPMorgan. Crowdstrike and Zscaler said that the deal will create the “largest single addressable market” for cybersecurity, which will enable the companies to better position themselves for the AI era.

The aim is to protect against hackers from stealing credentials and using them to gain unfettered access to a company’s network.

passages: Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the companies announced Monday.
Crowdstrike and Zscaler said that the deal will create the “largest single addressable market” for cybersecurity, which will enable the companies to better position themselves for the AI era.
Zscaler is a San Jose, Calif.-based tech company that provides cloud cybersecurity products to about 8,000 enterprise companies.
The company offers zero-trust technology, a security feature that requires employees to authenticate each and every time they access an internal system or resource.
The aim is to protect against hackers from stealing credentials and using them to gain unfettered access to a company’s network.

The aim is to protect against hackers from stealing credentials and using them to gain unfettered access to a company’s network. CrowdStrike, which secures the computers, laptops, phones and other devices connected to a company’s network, said the deal will unite its endpoint protection software with Zscaler’s zero-trust platform to better defend their customers against data breaches. In remarks on Monday, the companies said that the acquisition will help customers safely adopt AI. The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, is expected to close around this time next year.

passages: CrowdStrike is buying cloud security company Zscaler in an all-stock deal worth about $43.9 billion, the companies said Monday, in a major acquisition that combines two of the cybersecurity industry's biggest names.
CrowdStrike and Zscaler were already working together in a partnership that included 2,000 shared customers.
The deal would expand the combined company's market by more than $185 billion by 2029.
Zscaler shareholders will get 1.135 shares of Crowdstrike for each Zscaler share they own, under the deal's terms, which represent a 34% premium to Zscaler's closing price on Friday.
Crowdstrike's focus has been on so-called endpoint security, with services to protect laptops, mobile devices and desktop computers.
Santa Clara, California-based Zscaler, meanwhile, specializes in cloud-based network protection.
The transaction is expected to close in the second half of Crowdstrike's fiscal 2028 year, which begins in February.

Ever since his departure, speculation about the possibility of his return had been circulating across Silicon Valley. Even before his reinstatement, an online petition calling for his return as Nvidia CEO had gathered nearly 180,000 signatures, as prominent tech executives and shareholders rallied behind him following his resignation last week. Earlier reports from the Financial Times had also indicated that Huang's allies were assembling a war room of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his reinstatement and seek support from the White House. Following Huang's reinstatement, Elon Musk took to X and wrote: "The mistake has been corrected." In an earlier post, he had simply written: "It is done", without offering any explanation, seemingly hinting at the impending decision. extraction.body: You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates, and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees, a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable company. (The stock price has recently taken a tumble, for obvious reasons.) And now you’re back, baby — and all your friends are so eager to congratulate you. As a fellow leather jacket enthusiast who has a checkered history with women — including those who work for him — it’s clear that he and Huang have a lot in common beyond their positions as tech CEOs. President Donald Trump posted his lengthy congratulations to Huang on Truth Social. “I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote. He commended Nvidia’s board for making the “correct and proper” decision in reinstating Huang — a decision that, the board admits, was made with input “from senior levels of the United States government,” who determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no security risk.” Isn’t that great news? “I think you’re going to see some tremendous numbers out of this company,” Trump said on CNBC. I said, ‘Jensen, just promise me one thing: You’re going to work hard.’ I spoke to him last night because I knew what was going on.” The market’s reaction may be the most jubilant of all.

Ever since his departure, speculation about the possibility of his return had been circulating across Silicon Valley. Even before his reinstatement, an online petition calling for his return as Nvidia CEO had gathered nearly 180,000 signatures, as prominent tech executives and shareholders rallied behind him following his resignation last week. Beyond Nvidia employees, the "Stand with Jensen" campaign attracted support from Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. Musk had publicly backed the petition, calling for Jensen to return as the leading force behind Nvidia. Other supporters included Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke and former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick. Earlier reports from the Financial Times had also indicated that Huang's allies were assembling a war room of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his reinstatement and seek support from the White House. Following Huang's reinstatement, Elon Musk took to X and wrote: "The mistake has been corrected." In an earlier post, he had simply written: "It is done", without offering any explanation, seemingly hinting at the impending decision. The mistake has been corrected — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 23, 2026 Musk was joined by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who posted "Jensen" on X, signalling his support for Huang's reinstatement. Jensen! — Sam Altman (@sama) November 23, 2026 Steve Chen, co-founder of YouTube, also took to X to write: "JENSEN is Back". He described the development as a "Huge Win for Nvidia". Huge win for @nvidia, the entire AI industry, and builders everywhere. Let's go! — steve chen (@stevechen) November 23, 2026 While several tech leaders voiced support for the decision, others criticised the move to reinstate Huang amid an ongoing investigation. US Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren US Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren criticised Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang as CEO, calling it "reckless". She said the move did not absolve Huang, Nvidia's executives or its board of their responsibility to answer questions from Congress about the company's compliance with US export controls. This reckless decision to bring back Jensen Huang does not change the fact that Huang and NVIDIA still owe Congress answers. The Trump Administration needs to explain what "input" was given and by which senior officials to support Huang’s reinstatement. Huang’s return only increases the urgency to pass bipartisan export control bills and make sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk. — Elizabeth Warren (@SenWarren) November 23, 2026 Warren also called on the Trump administration to explain to Congress what role senior US government officials played in supporting Huang's reinstatement. She further argued that Huang's return made it more urgent for Congress to pass bipartisan export control legislation and ensure Nvidia did not lobby against measures that could put US national security at risk. Democratic Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi Democratic Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi also criticised the decision, calling Huang's reinstatement "outrageous" in a post on X. Trump’s assurances cannot be taken at face value, especially after Nvidia’s $25 million donation to his ballroom. Before Nvidia announced Huang's reinstatement, Shopify CEO Tobias Lutke had publicly questioned the company's board and its handling of the controversy surrounding the co-founder's departure. Speaking on an episode of David Senra's podcast released on Sunday, Luitke criticised the board's decision-making process and described the events leading to Huang's exit as highly orchestrated. The company said the decision followed consultations with senior US government officials. Huang’s exit had reportedly come amid concerns over his alleged affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence agencies of spying for China. His departure had unsettled financial markets and raised concerns about the impact on the artificial intelligence industry. Following the announcement of his return on Monday, US markets recovered, with Nvidia shares surging nearly 26% and the technology-heavy Nasdaq gaining more than 5%. US President Donald Trump, who had publicly called for Huang’s return, welcomed the board’s decision, describing it as a “correct and proper decision.” Nvidia said its board unanimously approved Huang’s return as president, CEO and board member with immediate effect. The company added that feedback from senior government officials helped address concerns about any potential national security implications of his reinstatement. Board Chair Harvey Jones said the directors remained convinced that Huang was the right choice to lead the company and that his return would benefit shareholders, employees, business partners and customers. Meanwhile, Jones will continue as board chair, while Colette Kress, who took over as interim CEO following Huang’s departure, will resume her responsibilities as chief financial officer.

That said, I’m delusionally holding out hope that the AirPods 5 will go on sale at some point next week.Best iPad DealsExpert tip: The best iPad deal up for grabs is $100 off the iPad Mini—though it dropped down to a record-low $349 during last year’s Black Friday sale. And even though you can score $150 off the 13-inch iPad Pro and $50 off the 11-inch iPad right now, both deals were significantly steeper last year. So, it’s possible that deals will be even better day-of.Best Apple Watch DealsExpert tip: Great news: the Apple Watch SE 3 returned to its record-low price of $199 and there’s a new lowest-ever deal on the Watch Series 12. That said, none of these laptops have hit record-low prices quite yet, so you stand to save more money if you wait for day-of deals.Best Apple Accessory DealsExpert tip: Last but not least, I spotted some gems in the accessories department. At $23 for one or $70 for a four-pack, the AirTag is on sale for its lowest price ever (and makes for a great holiday gift). Plus, you can save over 20% on the Apple Pencil, and USB-C charging cable.

sources.title: Nvidia reverses course and brings Jensen Huang back as CEO
passages: In a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board said on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, less than two weeks after he resigned following his admission of at least two extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman whom the U.S. government suspects to be a Chinese spy.
“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said. “I want to thank the Nvidia Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process.
I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading Nvidia during this period.
I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support.
Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family.
In the days since Huang resigned, President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his support for the ousted executive, who is now back at the helm of the AI chip giant.
Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.”

A long list of high-profile tech executives were pushing the board — in social media posts and publicly aired interviews — to bring Huang back, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Atoms founder Travis Kalanick, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan — all of whom signed a petition pushing for reinstatement.
Just a few days ago, the board had seemed immovable in its choice to push Huang out.
Jones said they didn’t intend reinstate Huang.
Nvidia had even retained executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.
Nvidia shares, which had already shot up in premarket trading, opened 30% higher.
Nvidia shares were priced at $159.95 a share, up 27%, at 9:51 am ET.
Jones, along with the rest of the board, now has a different view.

The decision marks an extraordinary comeback for one of the tech industry’s most influential executives, whose abrupt departure raised questions about national security and the future of the world’s most valuable chipmaker. Notably, the U.S. government itself played a role in his return: Nvidia’s board said it consulted senior government officials before determining that Huang posed no national security risk. Nvidia shares, which had already shot up in premarket trading, opened 30% higher. Nvidia shares were priced at $159.95 a share, up 27%, at 9:51 am ET. Trump said in a post on Truth Social that the board “made the correct and proper decision to return” Huang to the position, noting that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Nvidia poses any risk to national security. Trump also said the U.S. Attorney General confirmed that the U.S. government doesn’t have any evidence that Huang engaged in any illegal activity. A long list of high-profile tech executives were pushing the board — in social media posts and publicly aired interviews — to bring Huang back, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Atoms founder Travis Kalanick, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan — all of whom signed a petition pushing for reinstatement. The company said the board’s unanimous decision followed a series of discussions and meetings with Huang, after which they were “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.” Just a few days ago, the board had seemed immovable in its choice to push Huang out. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey C. Jones said they didn’t intend reinstate Huang. Nvidia had even retained executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement. Jones, along with the rest of the board, now has a different view. extraction.body: Just days after begging for his old job back and Nvidia’s Board of Directors saying that absolutely wasn’t going to happen, founder Jensen Huang has been made CEO again. It can’t be overstated just how much almost every serious tech business observer was saying just last week that there was basically zero chance of this happening . The shocking announcement comes just a day after Trump told the Board to un-fire Huang on Truth Social. The Board of Directors, led by Harvey Jones, had previously put CFO Colette Kress in charge of the company after firing Huang. “The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption,” Jones said at the time. That was less than two weeks ago. Here’s what he said in today’s announcement: “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.” He continued, “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company.” Why do I have every confidence that Jones is not confident about this? Nvidia writes that “the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Apparently the lynchpin of the entire AI bubble is under Trump’s thumb. The President, famous for telling people he’s been cleared of any wrongdoing , said his administration cleared Huang of any wrongdoing . To recap, Huang admitted to an affair with a Chinese national which U.S. intelligence reportedly believed could have been a spy. She seemed involved in a scheme to get Nvidia’s chips into China and to bypass current laws restrict that. But Huang has always been in favor of selling chips to China, and many in the AI-adjacent tech world think it’s good policy. It’s certainly good for the bottom lines of companies like Nvidia. But then reports started coming out about Huang’s additional affairs , specifically with two alleged Nvidia employees, something that seems likely to be in violation of company ethics policies. There is also the matter of what Huang did or didn’t inform Nvidia’s Board of Directors about related to all of this. They’re supposed to represent shareholders, and lying to them is a big no-no. Plus, with Democrats now in Congress, Huang is likely to face all sorts of hearings on Capitol Hill about the whole mess. Less than a week ago, Huang started lobbying to come back to Nvidia. The Board of Directors at the time said that possibility was not even under consideration, a stance that was reiterated during another blowout earnings report the same week. Something certainly changed between then and now. Was it just President Trump doubling down on pressuring the Board to bring Huang back? Whether this is actually good news for Nvidia as a company remains to be seen. At least Tim Sweeney will be happy . Here’s the press release announcement from Nvidia : Nvidia today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk. “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair. “I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.” As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it. The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries. Update 11/23/2026, 10:00 a.m. ET: Added the statement from the President. But Huang has always been in favor of selling chips to China, and many in the AI-adjacent tech world think it’s good policy. It’s certainly good for the bottom lines of companies like Nvidia.

But then reports started coming out about Huang’s additional affairs , specifically with two alleged Nvidia employees, something that seems likely to be in violation of company ethics policies. There is also the matter of what Huang did or didn’t inform Nvidia’s Board of Directors about related to all of this. They’re supposed to represent shareholders, and lying to them is a big no-no. Plus, with Democrats now in Congress, Huang is likely to face all sorts of hearings on Capitol Hill about the whole mess.

Less than a week ago, Huang started lobbying to come back to Nvidia. The Board of Directors at the time said that possibility was not even under consideration, a stance that was reiterated during another blowout earnings report the same week. Something certainly changed between then and now. Was it just President Trump doubling down on pressuring the Board to bring Huang back? Whether this is actually good news for Nvidia as a company remains to be seen. At least Tim Sweeney will be happy .
Here’s the press release announcement from Nvidia :

Nvidia today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”

As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.

The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

extraction.body: Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, reversing its decision to remove him less than two weeks ago following revelations about his personal relationships, including an alleged affair with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by U.S. authorities of having ties to Chinese intelligence. The decision follows mounting pressure from employees, investors, business partners and U.S. President Donald Trump, who publicly campaigned for Huang's return. The company said Monday that Huang's reinstatement takes effect immediately. Nvidia shares surged more than 31% in premarket trading following the announcement, reflecting investors' relief at the return of the executive who built the company into the world's dominant supplier of artificial intelligence processors. The decision marks an extraordinary reversal by Nvidia's board. On November 17, Chairman Harvey Jones said the board had unanimously accepted Huang's resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. The company had appointed longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and begun searching for a permanent replacement. Just days later, however, the pressure for Huang's return intensified. Trump repeatedly expressed support for the Nvidia founder, arguing that the company should take him back. A public petition calling for his reinstatement attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including support from Elon Musk, while employees, shareholders and business partners also urged the board to reconsider. According to Nvidia, the board is now satisfied with Huang's candor and leadership abilities. It also said that, after receiving input from senior U.S. government officials, it concluded that his return would pose no national security risk. Colette Kress will remain CFO, the company said. Huang resigned on November 12 after revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whom U.S. authorities suspect of having connections to Chinese intelligence. The controversy also involved reports of another relationship with a senior Nvidia employee who reportedly worked under Huang, raising questions about his conduct and the company's internal governance. In his first public statement following his departure, Huang acknowledged making serious mistakes in his personal life and apologized for creating problems for the board. He also said he would be willing to return if directors concluded that his reinstatement was in the company's best interests. At the time, however, the board appeared determined to move on without him. Huang's return comes after more than three decades at the helm of Nvidia, which he co-founded in 1993. Under his leadership, the company evolved from a designer of graphics processors for video games into the central supplier of chips powering the global AI industry. His influence extends beyond product development to major customer relationships, strategic investments in AI infrastructure companies and Nvidia's ties with Washington. The reversal also carries implications for Nvidia's substantial operations in Israel. The company employs approximately 6,200 people in the country, which has become one of its most important research and development centers outside the United States. Its Israeli teams play a central role in networking technology and other core products, much of which came through Nvidia's $6.9 billion acquisition of Mellanox in 2019. Huang was also a driving force behind the company's planned multibillion-shekel campus in Kiryat Tivon, which could eventually accommodate thousands of additional employees. The leadership crisis had raised questions about whether Nvidia would maintain the same level of commitment to its Israeli operations and expansion plans under a new CEO. Huang's reinstatement removes that immediate uncertainty, although the company will still have to address the governance and national security questions that led to his departure in the first place. The decision also comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia's business. The company reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, and forecast revenue of approximately $130 billion for the current quarter. Its results demonstrated that demand for AI processors remains exceptionally strong even as the company faced its most serious leadership crisis in decades. The board's decision to bring Huang back highlights the extraordinary influence he continues to wield over Nvidia, but also raises a broader question for investors: how much of the company's value and future success remains tied to a single executive.

Just a few days ago, the board had seemed immovable in its choice to push Huang out.
Jones said they didn’t intend reinstate Huang.
Nvidia had even retained executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.
Nvidia shares, which had already shot up in premarket trading, opened 30% higher.
Nvidia shares were priced at $159.95 a share, up 27%, at 9:51 am ET.
Jones, along with the rest of the board, now has a different view.

extraction.body: Just days after begging for his old job back and Nvidia’s Board of Directors saying that absolutely wasn’t going to happen, founder Jensen Huang has been made CEO again. It can’t be overstated just how much almost every serious tech business observer was saying just last week that there was basically zero chance of this happening . The shocking announcement comes just a day after Trump told the Board to un-fire Huang on Truth Social. The Board of Directors, led by Harvey Jones, had previously put CFO Colette Kress in charge of the company after firing Huang. “The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption,” Jones said at the time. That was less than two weeks ago. Here’s what he said in today’s announcement: “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.” He continued, “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company.” Why do I have every confidence that Jones is not confident about this? Nvidia writes that “the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Apparently the lynchpin of the entire AI bubble is under Trump’s thumb. The President, famous for telling people he’s been cleared of any wrongdoing , said his administration cleared Huang of any wrongdoing . To recap, Huang admitted to an affair with a Chinese national which U.S. intelligence reportedly believed could have been a spy. She seemed involved in a scheme to get Nvidia’s chips into China and to bypass current laws restrict that. But Huang has always been in favor of selling chips to China, and many in the AI-adjacent tech world think it’s good policy. It’s certainly good for the bottom lines of companies like Nvidia. But then reports started coming out about Huang’s additional affairs , specifically with two alleged Nvidia employees, something that seems likely to be in violation of company ethics policies. There is also the matter of what Huang did or didn’t inform Nvidia’s Board of Directors about related to all of this. They’re supposed to represent shareholders, and lying to them is a big no-no. Plus, with Democrats now in Congress, Huang is likely to face all sorts of hearings on Capitol Hill about the whole mess. Less than a week ago, Huang started lobbying to come back to Nvidia. The Board of Directors at the time said that possibility was not even under consideration, a stance that was reiterated during another blowout earnings report the same week. Something certainly changed between then and now. Was it just President Trump doubling down on pressuring the Board to bring Huang back? Whether this is actually good news for Nvidia as a company remains to be seen. At least Tim Sweeney will be happy . Here’s the press release announcement from Nvidia : Nvidia today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. passages: Just days after begging for his old job back and Nvidia’s Board of Directors saying that absolutely wasn’t going to happen, founder Jensen Huang has been made CEO again. It can’t be overstated just how much almost every serious tech business observer was saying just last week that there was basically zero chance of this happening . The shocking announcement comes just a day after Trump told the Board to un-fire Huang on Truth Social.

The Board of Directors, led by Harvey Jones, had previously put CFO Colette Kress in charge of the company after firing Huang. “The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption,” Jones said at the time. That was less than two weeks ago.

Here’s what he said in today’s announcement: “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.” He continued, “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company.” Why do I have every confidence that Jones is not confident about this?

Nvidia writes that “the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Apparently the lynchpin of the entire AI bubble is under Trump’s thumb. The President, famous for telling people he’s been cleared of any wrongdoing , said his administration cleared Huang of any wrongdoing .

To recap, Huang admitted to an affair with a Chinese national which U.S. intelligence reportedly believed could have been a spy. She seemed involved in a scheme to get Nvidia’s chips into China and to bypass current laws restrict that. But Huang has always been in favor of selling chips to China, and many in the AI-adjacent tech world think it’s good policy. It’s certainly good for the bottom lines of companies like Nvidia.

But then reports started coming out about Huang’s additional affairs , specifically with two alleged Nvidia employees, something that seems likely to be in violation of company ethics policies. There is also the matter of what Huang did or didn’t inform Nvidia’s Board of Directors about related to all of this. They’re supposed to represent shareholders, and lying to them is a big no-no. Plus, with Democrats now in Congress, Huang is likely to face all sorts of hearings on Capitol Hill about the whole mess.

Less than a week ago, Huang started lobbying to come back to Nvidia. The Board of Directors at the time said that possibility was not even under consideration, a stance that was reiterated during another blowout earnings report the same week. Something certainly changed between then and now. Was it just President Trump doubling down on pressuring the Board to bring Huang back? Whether this is actually good news for Nvidia as a company remains to be seen. At least Tim Sweeney will be happy .

extraction.body: Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, reversing its decision to remove him less than two weeks ago following revelations about his personal relationships, including an alleged affair with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by U.S. authorities of having ties to Chinese intelligence. The decision follows mounting pressure from employees, investors, business partners and U.S. President Donald Trump, who publicly campaigned for Huang's return. The company said Monday that Huang's reinstatement takes effect immediately. Nvidia shares surged more than 31% in premarket trading following the announcement, reflecting investors' relief at the return of the executive who built the company into the world's dominant supplier of artificial intelligence processors. The decision marks an extraordinary reversal by Nvidia's board. On November 17, Chairman Harvey Jones said the board had unanimously accepted Huang's resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. The company had appointed longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and begun searching for a permanent replacement. Just days later, however, the pressure for Huang's return intensified. Trump repeatedly expressed support for the Nvidia founder, arguing that the company should take him back. A public petition calling for his reinstatement attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including support from Elon Musk, while employees, shareholders and business partners also urged the board to reconsider. According to Nvidia, the board is now satisfied with Huang's candor and leadership abilities. It also said that, after receiving input from senior U.S. government officials, it concluded that his return would pose no national security risk. Colette Kress will remain CFO, the company said. Huang resigned on November 12 after revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whom U.S. authorities suspect of having connections to Chinese intelligence. The controversy also involved reports of another relationship with a senior Nvidia employee who reportedly worked under Huang, raising questions about his conduct and the company's internal governance. In his first public statement following his departure, Huang acknowledged making serious mistakes in his personal life and apologized for creating problems for the board. He also said he would be willing to return if directors concluded that his reinstatement was in the company's best interests. At the time, however, the board appeared determined to move on without him. Huang's return comes after more than three decades at the helm of Nvidia, which he co-founded in 1993. Under his leadership, the company evolved from a designer of graphics processors for video games into the central supplier of chips powering the global AI industry. His influence extends beyond product development to major customer relationships, strategic investments in AI infrastructure companies and Nvidia's ties with Washington. The reversal also carries implications for Nvidia's substantial operations in Israel. The company employs approximately 6,200 people in the country, which has become one of its most important research and development centers outside the United States. Its Israeli teams play a central role in networking technology and other core products, much of which came through Nvidia's $6.9 billion acquisition of Mellanox in 2019. Huang was also a driving force behind the company's planned multibillion-shekel campus in Kiryat Tivon, which could eventually accommodate thousands of additional employees. The leadership crisis had raised questions about whether Nvidia would maintain the same level of commitment to its Israeli operations and expansion plans under a new CEO. Huang's reinstatement removes that immediate uncertainty, although the company will still have to address the governance and national security questions that led to his departure in the first place. The decision also comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia's business. The company reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, and forecast revenue of approximately $130 billion for the current quarter. Its results demonstrated that demand for AI processors remains exceptionally strong even as the company faced its most serious leadership crisis in decades. The board's decision to bring Huang back highlights the extraordinary influence he continues to wield over Nvidia, but also raises a broader question for investors: how much of the company's value and future success remains tied to a single executive.

"President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses," White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said in a statement. Trump's message on Monday echoed that of Nvidia's board, which said in a statement that it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk." As Trump put it, Huang is needed "to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy." The turnabout comes after Trump and his team doubled down on supporting Huang in recent days and even criticized his replacements. Trump said during a press conference on Friday while discussing Huang's role in developing the company's advanced Blackwell chips: "Jensen did that, and I think there are very few people in that company that can do that." "I'm not trying to be disrespectful," Trump added of Huang's replacements. Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sharply reversed his position on Huang's ouster over the weekend. In a Sunday show appearance on CBS, Bessent backed away from his previous calls for fresh blood at the company when he quipped that "Jensen is on the outside now" and said he wanted to see "which level of the business" potentially endangered US national security. It was a departure from his comments last week when Bessent said the chipmaker needed "a dramatic shake-up." It was unclear Monday exactly what shape the various inquiries on Capitol Hill into Nvidia would take, but Democrats were quick to promise continued oversight when they take power in January. "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is in line to take over the Senate's banking committee, said in a statement in which she called Huang's reinstatement "a reckless decision." sources.title: DOT Sec. Duffy ties router in southern Arkansas to issues that led to nationwide ground stop - CNBC
passages: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that a router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies could be key to problems that led officials to order the biggest halt to flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 on Friday.
The equipment, along with another router that was in Amarillo, Texas, is at an L3Harris lab in Florida for examination, Duffy said.
It was the second time the FAA has issued a nationwide ground stop since the Sept.
Federal officials said on Saturday that "instability" in communication feeds and data like radar prompted the more than four-hour ground stop.

A few flights began to depart even before the ground stop was officially lifted; however, like trans-oceanic flights that were quickly handed off to other air traffic facilities, airlines had to seek approval for them one by one.
A router had "flooded" other routers in the air traffic control system with over 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, said Duffy.
Delta Air Lines offered crews double pay to pick up trips and gave them confirmed seats on flights to get them into position, according to internal company messages CNBC reviewed.
— CNBC's April Roach and Jessica Golden contributed to this article.

extraction.body: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that a router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies could be key to problems that led officials to order the biggest halt to flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 on Friday. "We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said in an interview with Fox News. "We're open if we see something else, we're going to continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement." Duffy told ABC's "This Week" in a separate interview that the router was located in El Dorado in southern Arkansas. The equipment, along with another router that was in Amarillo, Texas, is at an L3Harris lab in Florida for examination, Duffy said. He said the router, part of ongoing work to switch from copper wire to a fiber-optic system, began flooding other systems. Federal officials said on Saturday that "instability" in communication feeds and data like radar prompted the more than four-hour ground stop. Flight disruptions lingered on Sunday but were far from the thousands of cancellations passengers faced on Friday and Saturday. There was "zero evidence" that the problem was caused by something "nefarious" or anything related to artificial intelligence, Bryan Bedford, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, said at a press conference with Duffy Saturday morning. Bedford said no FAA facilities went dark but that officials decided to ground flights because of "instability" in information feeds to air traffic control centers that handle en route aircraft at high altitudes and eventually to others closer to airports. The issue occurred during "routine" upgrades of switching from a copper wire system to fiber, Bedford said. A router had "flooded" other routers in the air traffic control system with over 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, said Duffy. That created problems with airplane communications and radar feeds, they said. "We were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a center losing connectivity with aircraft," said Bedford. He said officials weren't sure for about 45 minutes what was causing the instability. The outage again thrust aging infrastructure that underpins U.S. air traffic control into the spotlight, along with the country's struggles to replace sections of it while operating the world's busiest airspace. "What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router," he said. L3Harris said it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel." The company, a longtime U.S. contractor, said it has completed more than 70% of the switch from copper wiring to fiber-optic system. Duffy took the groundstop to seek billions more from lawmakers to modernize the system. Flight disruptions began to ease Sunday, though more than 2,000 flights were canceled. That was down from the roughly 6,500 cancellations Saturday and over 8,000 delays, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. That's on top of more than 9,000 U.S. flight cancellations, about a third of the day's schedule, and more than 7,000 delays on Friday, though some disruptions were due to bad weather. Friday had the second-highest U.S. flight cancellations since a severe blizzard and below-freezing temperatures in January, according to aviation-data firm Cirium. Part of untangling from the ground stop included getting aircraft where they need to be. The ground stop forced many planes to divert to other airports, while dozens of planes had to park with limited gate space because flights couldn't depart. Airlines run one of the lightest schedules on Saturday and are deploying as many spare planes and crews as possible to get travelers and employees where they need to be as they're eager to start fresh for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday period. Delta Air Lines offered crews double pay to pick up trips and gave them confirmed seats on flights to get them into position, according to internal company messages CNBC reviewed. United Airlines was also offering pilots and flight attendants extra pay to pick up flights through Sunday, according to people familiar with the matter. American, along with other airlines, said it would change customers' tickets at no fee or fare difference if the outage affected their plans and that it would cap some airfares. Around 3 million people were scheduled to fly on Saturday, according to Cirium. The FAA had halted departing U.S. flights around 4 p.m. ET on Friday, a ground stop that lasted more than four hours, the longest such pause on departing flights in 25 years. A few flights began to depart even before the ground stop was officially lifted; however, like trans-oceanic flights that were quickly handed off to other air traffic facilities, airlines had to seek approval for them one by one. Duffy on Friday blamed outdated U.S. infrastructure for the problem and said Congress needs to approve more money to overhaul the country's air traffic control. Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have angered airline executives for years, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions. It was the second time the FAA has issued a nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks. Trump administration officials have repeatedly said it did not appear to be a cyberattack. "Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable," the FAA said late Friday. The disruption also upended travel for NBA, NHL and college teams , which struggled to reach their destinations in time for games this weekend. Duffy said Friday that college football teams traveling on charter flights could receive priority. "I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA to schedule their flight times and make sure they have games going off tomorrow," he said at the Friday night briefing. The Southeastern Conference announced on X that some games had been moved to Sunday due to the flight disruption. "We are in close communication with our member institutions to assess potential disruptions and coordinate appropriate responses," the SEC said in a statement shared on X. The National Football League said that it is putting in three backup referees for three games on Sunday because of the ground stop, "reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns." — CNBC's April Roach and Jessica Golden contributed to this article.

extraction.body: Darryl covers aviation and the FAA, and earlier this month, when the US suffered a sudden nationwide ground stop on air travel, Darryl was all over the story. He published a great report for us on The Verge about what happened, what and who was to blame, and what we might do about the underlying infrastructure failures in the aviation business. So ahead of Thanksgiving, one of the country’s major holiday travel weeks, I wanted to have Darryl on the show to walk us through this incident on Friday, November 13th, when the FAA grounded every departing flight in the country for more than four hours. You’ll hear us work backward from how a single router could cause this kind of damage to why our aviation infrastructure is so painfully out of date and what the government plans to do about it. Also, why incidents like this are creating a kind of swirling paranoia about AI and cyberattacks, even when the real culprit is far more mundane. Okay: aviation journalist Darryl Campbell on the FAA ground stop. We’ll have you back to talk about the book, but I feel like we’re going to use that idea to talk about air traffic control today on Decoder with you. Yeah, I think so much of what we’ve found out, even in the week since my report came out, has really just been a lot of boring management failures that have somehow cascaded to affect millions of people on thousands of flights. But what you’re referencing is the fact that you wrote a story for us about the nationwide ground stop the FAA had to call because of a bad router. You can sign up here. --- I’m going to take you back to Friday the 13th in a part of the country that nobody really associates with aviation, which is a little place called El Dorado, Arkansas. It’s the very tail end of part of this big backbone of data and telecommunications that’s really a private network run exclusively for air traffic control by a company called L3Harris, who runs it on behalf of the FAA. If you remember back in the ‘90s, early 2000s when you made your first switch from DSL to fiber optic, that is exactly what they’re trying to do there, except- So just to remind everybody, DSL ran on the phone lines. So I’m old enough to remember that, and maybe some of you out there are. And that sounds great, but in the private telecom world, that happens on entirely separate networks. Because you need that when you’re managing tens of thousands of flights every single day. One of the things that I think is really important to understand here is that the FAA runs its own private network. It was built by this contractor back in the ‘90s and early 2000s. Yeah, and that’s part of the challenge, because you have to have it to keep the aviation system going; you can’t just shut it down for a week, rip everything out, and replace it. You would think that they would know how to do a simple router swap without causing everything to go down, but that’s exactly what happened on Friday. If you go back and look at everything that exactly caused the outage, it’s like a comedy of errors. No single thing would have caused the entire system to crash, but every little missed opportunity, failed connection, or decision that somebody made with no knowledge of what happens downstream from everything, really led to the point where all of a sudden the most congested airspace in the world could not figure out where the airplanes were. They couldn’t talk to people who are en route, and that’s a serious safety problem that could have put thousands of people at risk. Let’s work backwards from the actual precipitating incident, and then let’s talk about the government’s response to this crisis. So there’s a router swap that happens in Arkansas. In your story, you say they swapped in a fiber router for an old copper router, and that thing started sending out too many requests for the network it was connected to. So L3Harris is trying to replace what is essentially a telephone switch from the 1960s with a new modern fiber optic data router. Now, if you’re on, let’s say, a perfectly modern networking system, and you’re switching out a fiber optic for a fiber optic line, the data routing is the same; the protocols that the routers use to communicate with each other are the same. Do you remember that DSL to fiber optic comparison we made? That’s not really an issue because everything can handle huge amounts of data with high throughput. When the manufacturer sends out these new routers, there’s a factory setting on it that says, “Okay, when you’re making a communication attempt for the first time, assume that you are doing it with a high-throughput fiber optic system.” L3Harris forgot to turn off that switch, and so as soon as they plug in- That’s it? Yeah, from what I can tell and from all the reports that have come out, that is literally it. So L3Harris has said, “Hey, we did what we were supposed to. The router manufacturer said everything was working as it’s supposed to. It’s just that someone forgot to say, ‘Hey, you’re connecting to an old system.’” So when it starts pinging what it thinks is a high-capacity fiber optic data network, it’s just sending thousands and thousands of communication requests. All these connection requests start displacing some of the normal data packets that come through the network, and you start losing a couple of data packets, and so maybe the image quality degrades, or the audio starts to skip or something like that. That’s fine if you’re just trying to talk to someone in a normal one-on-one setting.

That’s fine if you’re just trying to talk to someone in a normal one-on-one setting.
