extraction.body: An unprecedented telecommunications failure triggered a nationwide ground stop for nearly five hours Friday, stranding an estimated 1.5 million travelers across the United States and resulting in 9,814 flight delays and 5,117 cancellations. It also sparked a political firestorm as the Trump administration seized on the disruption as evidence that Congress should approve $50 billion for a sweeping overhaul of the country's air traffic control system, even as passengers remained stuck on parked planes and scrambled for rental cars, with their weekend travel plans thrown into chaos. U.S. airspace reopened at 8:15 p.m., but officials warned it would take days to clear the backlog. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin called the country's aging air traffic control infrastructure a "national security risk" and argued that years of congressional inaction had left the system vulnerable to the kind of failure that triggered Friday's nationwide ground stop. He simultaneously praised President Donald Trump's handling of the crisis. "This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like by the organization and the team he's put to handle crises like this," he said. "We’re moving at an unprecedented pace as a whole of government to make sure that we are doing the public justice by making sure everybody is safe, which everybody is." Former Republican Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene called the administration's response "a shakedown." He said controllers began receiving inconsistent information from radar systems and communications networks. That instability led officials to order the nationwide ground stop. Duffy said the disruption exposed the weaknesses of an air traffic control network that still relies on "old switches, old routers" and "1980s little copper lines." He said the FAA's legacy analogue telecommunications system became overloaded, causing instability in radar and communications data used by controllers. While newer IP-based systems continued to function, Duffy said, the failure of older equipment underscored the need for what he described as a "state-of-the-art air traffic control system" built with modern hardware, software and telecommunications technology. Duffy argued that the outage demonstrated why piecemeal upgrades were no longer sufficient to replace aging telecommunications infrastructure nationwide. He called on Congress to approve up to $50 billion to modernize the FAA's communications infrastructure, replace analogue technology with digital systems, upgrade software and telecommunications networks, and rebuild aging facilities. "New hardware, new software, new telecommunication," Duffy said, arguing that only a comprehensive rebuild would prevent future nationwide disruptions. The explanation didn't fly with Democrats. They questioned how the administration could shift the blame when they had been the majority for the past two years and half of Trump's first term. "You’ve literally controlled Congress for the past two years. And apparently, there’s always been money for vanity projects. But none to fix our air traffic control system? Perhaps Trump should prioritize aviation safety over his pathetic Arch," she wrote on X. Nick Langworthy, chairman of the Aviation Safety Caucus, warned against making this issue partisan. He said Friday's disruption demonstrated the urgent need to modernize the nation's aviation infrastructure and called on Congress to fund upgrades. "Funding this modernization is not a partisan issue," he wrote on X. "Congress must come together to make that funding a reality and ensure our air traffic control system has the modern equipment and reliable backup systems it needs." The FAA said it issued Friday's ground stop after communication issues affected multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers, and technicians were investigating the problem. "All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis," the FAA said in an advisory. Ken Gray, former pilot and intelligence officer, and now a professor at the University of New Haven, compared the fallout of the ground stop to that of the 9/11 terror attacks. "When 9/11 happened ... they did an incredible job getting planes down on the ground. They emptied the airspace out within two hours and got all the aircraft that were in the air on the ground," he said. "But once they got it all on the ground, it took several days for it to be safe to allow the aircraft back up. "Likewise, once they get everything back on the ground, even if everything is working again, it is going to take some time to get the aircraft back in towards their destinations because everything is out of sync as far as flights go." Steven Marks, managing partner of Podhurst Orseck, a leading aviation disaster litigation firm, predicted the ground stop would spark "chaos." "It is travel chaos because tomorrow many of these aircraft are going to be sitting at airports," he told Newsweek . "But they were not intended to land. So you're going to have problems with gates. You have problems with planes not even being able to find gates in certain airports." "So it's going to be everybody can be working all through the night to try and minimize the disruption, but it's going to occur." Marks also said that the U.S. was supposed to have the most "sophisticated aviation system in the world." A nationwide ground stop indicated a major issue, he said. "It's embarrassing, and it's dangerous, and it should never have happened," he said. "It presents a dangerous situation to the flying public. Not the disruption, but the safety of people's lives." "I suspect we'll get through the next 24 hours without any incidents, and hopefully that won't be the case. But it's a mess and it will be a mess for a few days," he continued, adding there was likely to be "worldwide disruptions." FBI officials referred inquiries by Newsweek to the Department of Homeland Security, which did not immediately return requests for comment late Friday. Marc Nichols, who served as FAA chief counsel under former President Joe Biden, told Newsweek that while ground stops are not atypical, nationwide orders are less common. "Ground stops are not unusual. Nationwide ground stops are a little more unusual," Nichols said. He explained that such measures could be implemented for several reasons, including anticipated weather, security concerns or system malfunctions. "At this stage, we should not speculate as to the cause," he said. Nichols added that the transportation secretary's statement suggested an air traffic control communications issue. "The FAA's primary concern is safety of passengers, and it will share more details with the public when appropriate," he said. Gray cited America's aging aviation system as a potential cause for the ground stop. "Our country has what is called critical infrastructure, those systems that if something were to happen to it, it makes it very difficult to continue on with day-to-day business. Well, communications is one such critical infrastructure, and that includes communications between systems like air traffic controllers," he told Newsweek . "The FAA is operating on old technology. So, if they have not updated their communication system, it's probably overdue."

extraction.body: Sean Duffy, the country’s transportation secretary, said his agency is ‘going to hold people accountable’. The top United States transportation official has said work being performed on an antiquated telecommunications system could be to blame for a rare, hours-long US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that halted all air traffic inside the country. At a news conference in Washington, DC, on Saturday, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy spoke about routine maintenance that was performed on Friday to upgrade a router from copper to fibre at a “very remote location”. Duffy said “contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment” caused the router in question to start flooding other ones in the country’s air traffic control system. “We had 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds,” he told reporters at the Department of Transportation. When those connection issues caused disruption in radar feeds and communications between air traffic controllers and aeroplanes, Duffy said a ground stop was ordered. “When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace,” he said. The Transportation Department identified the contractor of Friday’s maintenance as L3Harris, a US-based aerospace and defence company that has been tasked with modernising the communications system for the FAA. “What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it … installator error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?” Duffy said. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.” Duffy added that L3Harris, which he said had performed decades of work for the FAA, “didn’t meet the moment”. “They own this network. They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it,” he said. “Or was it a faulty router? And we’re going to find that out. And frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.” In response to Duffy’s allegations, L3Harris told Al Jazeera it has been working “in close coordination with the FAA” and places safety and reliability as its “highest priorities”. “We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the November 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” a spokesperson for the company said. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.” Amid concerns that Friday’s ground stop was the result of a cyberattack, the US government said Saturday it did not “believe” that was the cause. “Once we were able to isolate the work being done at this location, all of our systems came back online,” Duffy said. “So, we don’t believe this was cyber at all.” The head of the FAA, who also spoke at Saturday’s news conference, echoed the transportation secretary’s remarks, saying the system outage was caused by an equipment error. “We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said. A root cause analysis would be shared with the public when it is available, he added. As airlines and thousands of travellers begin the process of digging out from Friday’s groundstop, the longest and only second nationwide stop since 9/11, the FAA said full schedule integrity is expected by the end of Sunday. “We have crews and aircraft that are out of position for 12,000 flights that were lost,” Bedford said. “These crews, pilots and flight attendants need to get to their points of reconnection with their schedules.” Bedford said the FAA expects about 4,000 to 5,000 flights out of the 41,000 scheduled on Saturday to be cancelled. “That will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow,” he said. “I do think the worst is behind us.”

"We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said in an interview with Fox News. "We're open if we see something else, we're going to continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement." Duffy told ABC's "This Week" in a separate interview that the router was located in El Dorado in southern Arkansas. The equipment, along with another router that was in Amarillo, Texas, is at an L3Harris lab in Florida for examination, Duffy said. He said the router, part of ongoing work to switch from copper wire to a fiber-optic system, began flooding other systems. Federal officials said on Saturday that "instability" in communication feeds and data like radar prompted the more than four-hour ground stop. Flight disruptions lingered on Sunday but were far from the thousands of cancellations passengers faced on Friday and Saturday. There was "zero evidence" that the problem was caused by something "nefarious" or anything related to artificial intelligence, Bryan Bedford, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, said at a press conference with Duffy Saturday morning. Bedford said no FAA facilities went dark but that officials decided to ground flights because of "instability" in information feeds to air traffic control centers that handle en route aircraft at high altitudes and eventually to others closer to airports. The issue occurred during "routine" upgrades of switching from a copper wire system to fiber, Bedford said. A router had "flooded" other routers in the air traffic control system with over 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, said Duffy. That created problems with airplane communications and radar feeds, they said. "We were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a center losing connectivity with aircraft," said Bedford. He said officials weren't sure for about 45 minutes what was causing the instability. The outage again thrust aging infrastructure that underpins U.S. air traffic control into the spotlight, along with the country's struggles to replace sections of it while operating the world's busiest airspace. "What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router," he said. L3Harris said it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel." The company, a longtime U.S. contractor, said it has completed more than 70% of the switch from copper wiring to fiber-optic system. Duffy took the groundstop to seek billions more from lawmakers to modernize the system. Flight disruptions began to ease Sunday, though more than 2,000 flights were canceled. That was down from the roughly 6,500 cancellations Saturday and over 8,000 delays, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. That's on top of more than 9,000 U.S. flight cancellations, about a third of the day's schedule, and more than 7,000 delays on Friday, though some disruptions were due to bad weather. Friday had the second-highest U.S. flight cancellations since a severe blizzard and below-freezing temperatures in January, according to aviation-data firm Cirium. Part of untangling from the ground stop included getting aircraft where they need to be. The ground stop forced many planes to divert to other airports, while dozens of planes had to park with limited gate space because flights couldn't depart. Airlines run one of the lightest schedules on Saturday and are deploying as many spare planes and crews as possible to get travelers and employees where they need to be as they're eager to start fresh for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday period. Delta Air Lines offered crews double pay to pick up trips and gave them confirmed seats on flights to get them into position, according to internal company messages CNBC reviewed. United Airlines was also offering pilots and flight attendants extra pay to pick up flights through Sunday, according to people familiar with the matter. American, along with other airlines, said it would change customers' tickets at no fee or fare difference if the outage affected their plans and that it would cap some airfares. Around 3 million people were scheduled to fly on Saturday, according to Cirium. Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have angered airline executives for years, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions. It was the second time the FAA has issued a nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks. Trump administration officials have repeatedly said it did not appear to be a cyberattack. "Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable," the FAA said late Friday. The disruption also upended travel for NBA, NHL and college teams , which struggled to reach their destinations in time for games this weekend. Duffy said Friday that college football teams traveling on charter flights could receive priority. "I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA to schedule their flight times and make sure they have games going off tomorrow," he said at the Friday night briefing. The Southeastern Conference announced on X that some games had been moved to Sunday due to the flight disruption. "We are in close communication with our member institutions to assess potential disruptions and coordinate appropriate responses," the SEC said in a statement shared on X. The National Football League said that it is putting in three backup referees for three games on Sunday because of the ground stop, "reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns." — CNBC's April Roach and Jessica Golden contributed to this article.

extraction.body: Darryl covers aviation and the FAA, and earlier this month, when the US suffered a sudden nationwide ground stop on air travel, Darryl was all over the story. He published a great report for us on The Verge about what happened, what and who was to blame, and what we might do about the underlying infrastructure failures in the aviation business. So ahead of Thanksgiving, one of the country’s major holiday travel weeks, I wanted to have Darryl on the show to walk us through this incident on Friday, November 13th, when the FAA grounded every departing flight in the country for more than four hours. You’ll hear us work backward from how a single router could cause this kind of damage to why our aviation infrastructure is so painfully out of date and what the government plans to do about it. Also, why incidents like this are creating a kind of swirling paranoia about AI and cyberattacks, even when the real culprit is far more mundane. Okay: aviation journalist Darryl Campbell on the FAA ground stop. We’ll have you back to talk about the book, but I feel like we’re going to use that idea to talk about air traffic control today on Decoder with you. Yeah, I think so much of what we’ve found out, even in the week since my report came out, has really just been a lot of boring management failures that have somehow cascaded to affect millions of people on thousands of flights. But what you’re referencing is the fact that you wrote a story for us about the nationwide ground stop the FAA had to call because of a bad router. You can sign up here. --- I’m going to take you back to Friday the 13th in a part of the country that nobody really associates with aviation, which is a little place called El Dorado, Arkansas. It’s the very tail end of part of this big backbone of data and telecommunications that’s really a private network run exclusively for air traffic control by a company called L3Harris, who runs it on behalf of the FAA. If you remember back in the ‘90s, early 2000s when you made your first switch from DSL to fiber optic, that is exactly what they’re trying to do there, except- So just to remind everybody, DSL ran on the phone lines. So I’m old enough to remember that, and maybe some of you out there are. And that sounds great, but in the private telecom world, that happens on entirely separate networks. Because you need that when you’re managing tens of thousands of flights every single day. One of the things that I think is really important to understand here is that the FAA runs its own private network. It was built by this contractor back in the ‘90s and early 2000s. Yeah, and that’s part of the challenge, because you have to have it to keep the aviation system going; you can’t just shut it down for a week, rip everything out, and replace it. You would think that they would know how to do a simple router swap without causing everything to go down, but that’s exactly what happened on Friday. If you go back and look at everything that exactly caused the outage, it’s like a comedy of errors. No single thing would have caused the entire system to crash, but every little missed opportunity, failed connection, or decision that somebody made with no knowledge of what happens downstream from everything, really led to the point where all of a sudden the most congested airspace in the world could not figure out where the airplanes were. They couldn’t talk to people who are en route, and that’s a serious safety problem that could have put thousands of people at risk. Let’s work backwards from the actual precipitating incident, and then let’s talk about the government’s response to this crisis. So there’s a router swap that happens in Arkansas. In your story, you say they swapped in a fiber router for an old copper router, and that thing started sending out too many requests for the network it was connected to. So L3Harris is trying to replace what is essentially a telephone switch from the 1960s with a new modern fiber optic data router. Now, if you’re on, let’s say, a perfectly modern networking system, and you’re switching out a fiber optic for a fiber optic line, the data routing is the same; the protocols that the routers use to communicate with each other are the same. Do you remember that DSL to fiber optic comparison we made? That’s not really an issue because everything can handle huge amounts of data with high throughput. When the manufacturer sends out these new routers, there’s a factory setting on it that says, “Okay, when you’re making a communication attempt for the first time, assume that you are doing it with a high-throughput fiber optic system.” L3Harris forgot to turn off that switch, and so as soon as they plug in- That’s it? Yeah, from what I can tell and from all the reports that have come out, that is literally it. So L3Harris has said, “Hey, we did what we were supposed to. The router manufacturer said everything was working as it’s supposed to. It’s just that someone forgot to say, ‘Hey, you’re connecting to an old system.’” So when it starts pinging what it thinks is a high-capacity fiber optic data network, it’s just sending thousands and thousands of communication requests. All these connection requests start displacing some of the normal data packets that come through the network, and you start losing a couple of data packets, and so maybe the image quality degrades, or the audio starts to skip or something like that. That’s fine if you’re just trying to talk to someone in a normal one-on-one setting.

extraction.body: An unprecedented telecommunications failure triggered a nationwide ground stop for nearly five hours Friday, stranding an estimated 1.5 million travelers across the United States and resulting in 9,814 flight delays and 5,117 cancellations. It also sparked a political firestorm as the Trump administration seized on the disruption as evidence that Congress should approve $50 billion for a sweeping overhaul of the country's air traffic control system, even as passengers remained stuck on parked planes and scrambled for rental cars, with their weekend travel plans thrown into chaos. U.S. airspace reopened at 8:15 p.m., but officials warned it would take days to clear the backlog. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin called the country's aging air traffic control infrastructure a "national security risk" and argued that years of congressional inaction had left the system vulnerable to the kind of failure that triggered Friday's nationwide ground stop. He simultaneously praised President Donald Trump's handling of the crisis. "This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like by the organization and the team he's put to handle crises like this," he said. "We’re moving at an unprecedented pace as a whole of government to make sure that we are doing the public justice by making sure everybody is safe, which everybody is." Former Republican Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene called the administration's response "a shakedown." He said controllers began receiving inconsistent information from radar systems and communications networks. That instability led officials to order the nationwide ground stop. Duffy said the disruption exposed the weaknesses of an air traffic control network that still relies on "old switches, old routers" and "1980s little copper lines." He said the FAA's legacy analogue telecommunications system became overloaded, causing instability in radar and communications data used by controllers. While newer IP-based systems continued to function, Duffy said, the failure of older equipment underscored the need for what he described as a "state-of-the-art air traffic control system" built with modern hardware, software and telecommunications technology. Duffy argued that the outage demonstrated why piecemeal upgrades were no longer sufficient to replace aging telecommunications infrastructure nationwide. He called on Congress to approve up to $50 billion to modernize the FAA's communications infrastructure, replace analogue technology with digital systems, upgrade software and telecommunications networks, and rebuild aging facilities. "New hardware, new software, new telecommunication," Duffy said, arguing that only a comprehensive rebuild would prevent future nationwide disruptions. The explanation didn't fly with Democrats. They questioned how the administration could shift the blame when they had been the majority for the past two years and half of Trump's first term. "You’ve literally controlled Congress for the past two years. And apparently, there’s always been money for vanity projects. But none to fix our air traffic control system? Perhaps Trump should prioritize aviation safety over his pathetic Arch," she wrote on X. Nick Langworthy, chairman of the Aviation Safety Caucus, warned against making this issue partisan. He said Friday's disruption demonstrated the urgent need to modernize the nation's aviation infrastructure and called on Congress to fund upgrades. "Funding this modernization is not a partisan issue," he wrote on X. "Congress must come together to make that funding a reality and ensure our air traffic control system has the modern equipment and reliable backup systems it needs." The FAA said it issued Friday's ground stop after communication issues affected multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers, and technicians were investigating the problem. "All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis," the FAA said in an advisory. Ken Gray, former pilot and intelligence officer, and now a professor at the University of New Haven, compared the fallout of the ground stop to that of the 9/11 terror attacks. "When 9/11 happened ... they did an incredible job getting planes down on the ground. They emptied the airspace out within two hours and got all the aircraft that were in the air on the ground," he said. "But once they got it all on the ground, it took several days for it to be safe to allow the aircraft back up. "Likewise, once they get everything back on the ground, even if everything is working again, it is going to take some time to get the aircraft back in towards their destinations because everything is out of sync as far as flights go." Steven Marks, managing partner of Podhurst Orseck, a leading aviation disaster litigation firm, predicted the ground stop would spark "chaos." "It is travel chaos because tomorrow many of these aircraft are going to be sitting at airports," he told Newsweek . "But they were not intended to land. So you're going to have problems with gates. You have problems with planes not even being able to find gates in certain airports." "So it's going to be everybody can be working all through the night to try and minimize the disruption, but it's going to occur." Marks also said that the U.S. was supposed to have the most "sophisticated aviation system in the world." A nationwide ground stop indicated a major issue, he said. "It's embarrassing, and it's dangerous, and it should never have happened," he said. "It presents a dangerous situation to the flying public. Not the disruption, but the safety of people's lives." "I suspect we'll get through the next 24 hours without any incidents, and hopefully that won't be the case. But it's a mess and it will be a mess for a few days," he continued, adding there was likely to be "worldwide disruptions." FBI officials referred inquiries by Newsweek to the Department of Homeland Security, which did not immediately return requests for comment late Friday. Marc Nichols, who served as FAA chief counsel under former President Joe Biden, told Newsweek that while ground stops are not atypical, nationwide orders are less common. "Ground stops are not unusual. Nationwide ground stops are a little more unusual," Nichols said. He explained that such measures could be implemented for several reasons, including anticipated weather, security concerns or system malfunctions. "At this stage, we should not speculate as to the cause," he said. Nichols added that the transportation secretary's statement suggested an air traffic control communications issue. "The FAA's primary concern is safety of passengers, and it will share more details with the public when appropriate," he said. Gray cited America's aging aviation system as a potential cause for the ground stop. "Our country has what is called critical infrastructure, those systems that if something were to happen to it, it makes it very difficult to continue on with day-to-day business. Well, communications is one such critical infrastructure, and that includes communications between systems like air traffic controllers," he told Newsweek . "The FAA is operating on old technology. So, if they have not updated their communication system, it's probably overdue."

extraction.body: Sean Duffy, the country’s transportation secretary, said his agency is ‘going to hold people accountable’. The top United States transportation official has said work being performed on an antiquated telecommunications system could be to blame for a rare, hours-long US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that halted all air traffic inside the country. At a news conference in Washington, DC, on Saturday, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy spoke about routine maintenance that was performed on Friday to upgrade a router from copper to fibre at a “very remote location”. Duffy said “contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment” caused the router in question to start flooding other ones in the country’s air traffic control system. “We had 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds,” he told reporters at the Department of Transportation. When those connection issues caused disruption in radar feeds and communications between air traffic controllers and aeroplanes, Duffy said a ground stop was ordered. “When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace,” he said. The Transportation Department identified the contractor of Friday’s maintenance as L3Harris, a US-based aerospace and defence company that has been tasked with modernising the communications system for the FAA. “What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it … installator error from L3Harris? They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it,” he said. “Or was it a faulty router? And we’re going to find that out. The top United States transportation official has said work being performed on an antiquated telecommunications system could be to blame for a rare, hours-long US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that halted all air traffic inside the country.

At a news conference in Washington, DC, on Saturday, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy spoke about routine maintenance that was performed on Friday to upgrade a router from copper to fibre at a “very remote location”.
Duffy said “contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment” caused the router in question to start flooding other ones in the country’s air traffic control system.
“We had 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds,” he told reporters at the Department of Transportation.
When those connection issues caused disruption in radar feeds and communications between air traffic controllers and aeroplanes, Duffy said a ground stop was ordered.
“When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace,” he said.

The Transportation Department identified the contractor of Friday’s maintenance as L3Harris, a US-based aerospace and defence company that has been tasked with modernising the communications system for the FAA.

“What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it … installator error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?” Duffy said. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”
Duffy added that L3Harris, which he said had performed decades of work for the FAA, “didn’t meet the moment”.

“They own this network. They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it,” he said. “Or was it a faulty router? And we’re going to find that out. And frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.”
In response to Duffy’s allegations, L3Harris told Al Jazeera it has been working “in close coordination with the FAA” and places safety and reliability as its “highest priorities”.

“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the November 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” a spokesperson for the company said. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”
Amid concerns that Friday’s ground stop was the result of a cyberattack, the US government said Saturday it did not “believe” that was the cause.

“We have crews and aircraft that are out of position for 12,000 flights that were lost,” Bedford said. “These crews, pilots and flight attendants need to get to their points of reconnection with their schedules.”
Bedford said the FAA expects about 4,000 to 5,000 flights out of the 41,000 scheduled on Saturday to be cancelled.
“That will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow,” he said. “I do think the worst is behind us.”

In his comments on Monday, Trump claimed that U.S. Attorney General [Todd Blanche] had found no evidence that Mr. Huang had engaged in unlawful conduct. It’s an unusual statement for a U.S. president to make, as the attorney general typically conducts those investigations independently. Ms. Huang was an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, which had purchased billions in Nvidia chips over the past couple of years. This relationship had raised national security concerns about whether the CEO ties to Ms. Huang could have compromised sensitive information or facilitated China’s access to advanced U.S. AI chips, which are subject to export restrictions. Trump said last week that he believed this relationship didn’t threaten the U.S.’s national security, and instead said that no one had proven she’s a spy. “She may not be a spy,” the president said, adding that “China plays games with us, and we play games with China.” Trump’s full statement on Huang’s return, released on Monday, is below. He told CNBC in a phone interview Monday about his call to the board. "I spoke to them and I convinced them," he said. "And it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week ago." The president also claimed in a Truth Social post Monday that the U.S. government "has no reason to believe" that Huang's return to Nvidia as CEO "poses any risk to national security," although he did not elaborate. His social media comment went up shortly after Nvidia announced its board had reinstated Huang. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. The president said Nvidia's board asked "for assurance on the national security threat" and he gave them "assurance." The president told CNBC he believes his intervention was essential to getting Huang reinstated. It’s an unusual statement for a U.S. president to make, as the attorney general typically conducts those investigations independently. Ms. Huang was an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, which had purchased billions in Nvidia chips over the past couple of years. This relationship had raised national security concerns about whether the CEO ties to Ms. Huang could have compromised sensitive information or facilitated China’s access to advanced U.S. AI chips, which are subject to export restrictions. Trump said last week that he believed this relationship didn’t threaten the U.S.’s national security, and instead said that no one had proven she’s a spy. “She may not be a spy,” the president said, adding that “China plays games with us, and we play games with China.” Trump’s full statement on Huang’s return, released on Monday, is below. Meanwhile, Republican Senator John Cornyn challenged Trump's assurance to Nvidia that Huang posed no security threat. President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia.

That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China.

extraction.body: Trump says he spoke to the board and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals . The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures. Huang had been seeking a return to Nvidia since shortly after his resignation, reportedly forming a war room to strategize how best to bring it to pass. Last week, Huang posted on social media that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” he wrote on Truth Social last week. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” In a social media post immediately following the reinstatement, Trump called it “the correct and proper decision” and confirmed that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” Appearing on CNBC Monday morning , Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that… he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents,” Trump said. “You have to protect our geniuses and there aren’t enough of them.” Huang’s tenure at Nvidia dates back to the company’s founding in 1993, when he and three cofounders were focused on the then-nascent field of GPU hardware aimed at PC gamers. In the decades since, the highly parallel cores in those GPUs have been embraced first by cryptocurrency miners and then AI companies, propelling the company to its position as the most valuable in the world at its October peak. Nvidia stock—the price of which had sunk roughly 25 percent since Huang’s resignation was announced and nearly 50 percent since its peak—was up about 30 percent in early morning trading in the immediate aftermath of Huang’s reinstatement announcement. Huang’s return in some ways echoes that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was fired almost exactly three years ago after the board said it “no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.” Two weeks later, Altman was back at the helm after many employees threatened a mass revolt and departure if he wasn’t brought back. In Huang’s case, the revolt following his departure came not from employees but from fellow titans of the tech industry. Executives including Altman, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey are among the prominent industry figures who have publicly offered him support in the days since his resignation. In its statement, the Nvidia board reiterated that it has retained independent counsel and formed a committee of independent directors to investigate what it calls Huang’s targeting by “a foreign intelligence effort.” The company has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and is seeking to hire a new chief compliance officer position. This story has been updated to reflect Trump’s statements to CNBC.

passages: President Donald Trump said he spoke with Nvidia’s board members about reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, telling CNBC this morning that he sought to provide assurances to address their concerns about national security.
“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” Trump said Monday.

Asked on CNBC about Republican lawmakers who might be concerned with Huang’s return, Trump said, “When I speak to them, they’re going to be great.” Asked how he would respond to people who questioned why a president should get involve in the governance of a company like Nvidia, Trump said, “I’m doing it for the country.” Trump did not provide specific markers on how he would determine whether to get involved in an American company.
He knows what to do and what not to do.” Earlier Monday, Nvidia said in a statement that it had received assurances about Huang from the U.S. government, though it did not name Trump.
Trump also expressed concern that if Huang was not reinstated, China could try to recruit him to work for a Chinese company.

“The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me.” The president initially supported the idea of former Apple CEO Tim Cook being brought on to run Nvidia before he endorsed Huang’s return.
Trump told CNBC that he did not think “anybody can do” what Huang does, referring to the company’s prospects moving forward.
“If we didn’t do this, I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, “Hey, how would you like to come to China?” Trump said.
Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Huang quickly drew blowback from the president’s critics on both sides of the aisle.

Huang’s reinstatement at the top of Nvidia sent stocks surging after the market slid last week. In the nearly hourlong interview, Trump cast himself as a central figure in Huang’s reinstatement, saying he spoke with the key players involved in the company. The president added that he spoke with Huang “after I made the deal, after the deal was finished.” “I called him up and I said, ‘I ask you to do one thing, Jensen, work hard,’” Trump said. “I didn’t talk about other things because he understands that. The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures. Huang had been seeking a return to Nvidia since shortly after his resignation, reportedly forming a war room to strategize how best to bring it to pass. Last week, Huang posted on social media that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” he wrote on Truth Social last week. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” In a social media post immediately following the reinstatement, Trump called it “the correct and proper decision” and confirmed that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” Appearing on CNBC Monday morning , Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that… he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents,” Trump said. “You have to protect our geniuses and there aren’t enough of them.” Huang’s tenure at Nvidia dates back to the company’s founding in 1993, when he and three cofounders were focused on the then-nascent field of GPU hardware aimed at PC gamers. In the decades since, the highly parallel cores in those GPUs have been embraced first by cryptocurrency miners and then AI companies, propelling the company to its position as the most valuable in the world at its October peak. Nvidia stock—the price of which had sunk roughly 25 percent since Huang’s resignation was announced and nearly 50 percent since its peak—was up about 30 percent in early morning trading in the immediate aftermath of Huang’s reinstatement announcement. Huang’s return in some ways echoes that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was fired almost exactly three years ago after the board said it “no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.” Two weeks later, Altman was back at the helm after many employees threatened a mass revolt and departure if he wasn’t brought back. In Huang’s case, the revolt following his departure came not from employees but from fellow titans of the tech industry. Executives including Altman, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey are among the prominent industry figures who have publicly offered him support in the days since his resignation. In its statement, the Nvidia board reiterated that it has retained independent counsel and formed a committee of independent directors to investigate what it calls Huang’s targeting by “a foreign intelligence effort.” The company has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and is seeking to hire a new chief compliance officer position. passages: US President Donald Trump called on former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang to issue a major apology and return to lead the chipmaker giant, expressing confidence in his leadership despite the company's board showing no indication that it intends to reverse its decision.
Contributor at SEE News — Sada Elbalad English.

Speaking during a press conference at the White House on Friday, November 20, Trump described Huang as "one of the brightest and most exceptional minds in the world", arguing that his return would benefit both Nvidia and the United States.
However, he reiterated his preference for giving Huang another opportunity, saying: "I would like Jensen to be given a second chance.
Trump also disclosed that he had raised Huang's situation with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their meeting in Shenzhen earlier this week.

Huang's departure followed reports concerning an alleged romantic relationship with a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence, who reportedly worked for a Singapore-based company that obtained advanced Nvidia chips.
Trump, meanwhile, dismissed concerns that the Nvidia controversy had compromised American national security.
Trump's intervention comes at a particularly sensitive moment for Nvidia, whose shares have come under significant pressure amid corporate leadership uncertainty and reports of regulatory scrutiny.

extraction.body: US President Donald Trump called on former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang to issue a major apology and return to lead the chipmaker giant, expressing confidence in his leadership despite the company's board showing no indication that it intends to reverse its decision. Speaking during a press conference at the White House on Friday, November 20, Trump described Huang as "one of the brightest and most exceptional minds in the world", arguing that his return would benefit both Nvidia and the United States. "I want Jensen to make a big apology and come back. He brought us to a point where we're 10 years ahead of everybody else," Trump said. While advocating for Huang's return, Trump revealed that his personal choice to replace the former Nvidia chief executive would be Apple CEO Tim Cook. However, he reiterated his preference for giving Huang another opportunity, saying: "I would like Jensen to be given a second chance. We are a country that believes in second chances." Nvidia's board, however, has indicated that it does not intend to reinstate Huang following his departure, leaving the possibility of a leadership comeback uncertain. Trump also disclosed that he had raised Huang's situation with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their meeting in Shenzhen earlier this week. According to Trump, Xi also described Huang as a "genius", highlighting the semiconductor executive's international standing and importance to the global technology industry. Huang's departure followed reports concerning an alleged romantic relationship with a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence, who reportedly worked for a Singapore-based company that obtained advanced Nvidia chips. The controversy has also exposed disagreements within the US administration over its approach to China and restrictions on semiconductor exports. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly criticised the Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, accusing it of failing to prevent China from obtaining advanced technologies. Trump, meanwhile, dismissed concerns that the Nvidia controversy had compromised American national security. "China plays with us, and we play with China," he told reporters before departing on his trip. Trump's intervention comes at a particularly sensitive moment for Nvidia, whose shares have come under significant pressure amid corporate leadership uncertainty and reports of regulatory scrutiny. His public support for Huang adds another political dimension to the company's challenges, raising questions about the potential influence of Washington's technology policy on one of America's most strategically important semiconductor businesses. For now, however, Nvidia's board has given no indication that it plans to bring its former chief executive back. Contributor at SEE News — Sada Elbalad English. While advocating for Huang's return, Trump revealed that his personal choice to replace the former Nvidia chief executive would be Apple CEO Tim Cook.
However, he reiterated his preference for giving Huang another opportunity, saying: "I would like Jensen to be given a second chance. We are a country that believes in second chances."

Trump also disclosed that he had raised Huang's situation with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their meeting in Shenzhen earlier this week.

The dinner, held at the Trump National golf club in Sterling, Virginia, comes as some Democrats say they will investigate potential conflicts of interest and accuse Trump of using the presidency to boost his personal wealth. At Sunday's dinner, Trump maintained that his support for cryptocurrencies was to boost American economic competitiveness. "I'm doing it for the United States ... If we don't do it, China's going to do it," he told attendees, The Guardian reported. The event also featured speeches from boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary and NBA champion Tristan Thompson. A total of 185 "wallets" met the criteria for entry to the gala, although the leaderboard on the $TRUMP coin club website listed just 130 wallets. The wallets listed on the leaderboard held $8.6 million in $TRUMP tokens, a sharp decline from the May 2025 gala, which featured 220 attendees holding a combined $148 million. Crypto billionaire Justin Sun's wallet alone held $18.5 million at the 2025 event — more than the combined holdings of this year's attendees. Eligibility was based on time-weighted holdings of Trump's meme coins from Sept. 30 to Nov. 16, according to the organizer's website. The top 29 holders were invited to a VIP reception with the president, with the top four receiving an 18-karat, Trump-branded gold watch. More than half of the wallets that qualified for the event were linked to crypto exchanges that bar U.S.-based users, according to data gathered by consumer advocacy group Public Citizen for Reuters , suggesting they belong to foreign nationals. The $TRUMP token has earned the Trump family at least $635 million, according to the president's June financial disclosure. Including the meme coins, the Trump family has earned $2.3 billion from its four main crypto-related businesses since the president's second term began, through to April of this year, according to a Reuters report. This is despite the ventures' falling value, which, according to the report, they invest little to no money in. Trump's stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group , is worth about $430 million as of Friday's close. Bitcoin fell as low as $55,130 on Saturday, its lowest level since September 2024. The sell-off wiped out $1.8 billion in leveraged crypto positions, largely from bets on prices rising. Leveraged buyers were forced out as prices fell, then returned after the price stabilized. The world's largest cryptocurrency is still trading at less than half of its October 2025 value. The dinner, held at the Trump National golf club in Sterling, Virginia, comes as some Democrats say they will investigate potential conflicts of interest and accuse Trump of using the presidency to boost his personal wealth. At Sunday's dinner, Trump maintained that his support for cryptocurrencies was to boost American economic competitiveness. "I'm doing it for the United States ... If we don't do it, China's going to do it," he told attendees, The Guardian reported. The event also featured speeches from boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary and NBA champion Tristan Thompson. A total of 185 "wallets" met the criteria for entry to the gala, although the leaderboard on the $TRUMP coin club website listed just 130 wallets. The wallets listed on the leaderboard held $8.6 million in $TRUMP tokens, a sharp decline from the May 2025 gala, which featured 220 attendees holding a combined $148 million. Crypto billionaire Justin Sun's wallet alone held $18.5 million at the 2025 event — more than the combined holdings of this year's attendees. Eligibility was based on time-weighted holdings of Trump's meme coins from Sept. 30 to Nov. 16, according to the organizer's website. The top 29 holders were invited to a VIP reception with the president, with the top four receiving an 18-karat, Trump-branded gold watch. More than half of the wallets that qualified for the event were linked to crypto exchanges that bar U.S.-based users, according to data gathered by consumer advocacy group Public Citizen for Reuters , suggesting they belong to foreign nationals. The $TRUMP token has earned the Trump family at least $635 million, according to the president's June financial disclosure. Including the meme coins, the Trump family has earned $2.3 billion from its four main crypto-related businesses since the president's second term began, through to April of this year, according to a Reuters report. passages: Nvidia on Monday reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive in a stunning reversal that President Donald Trump said followed his own direct contacts with the company's board.

Board chair Harvey Jones said directors believe Huang "is the right person to lead Nvidia" and that his return serves the interests of shareholders, employees, partners and customers.

Huang, 63, stepped down after reports that he had a relationship with Alice Huang -- no relation -- a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company that bought billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips.

Nvidia said a committee of independent directors set up earlier this month to investigate whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort will see its probe through to the end, and that Huang has committed to cooperating.

Nvidia was also among the largest donors to Trump's White House ballroom project, contributing $25 million, according to a donor list published by The Washington Post last month.

His comeback followed a campaign by Silicon Valley figures including Elon Musk, while thousands of current and former Nvidia employees signed an open letter calling for his reinstatement.
Jones will remain chair, and chief financial officer Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will continue as CFO.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded. Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy . But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet. Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat. "In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday. Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China . Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal. The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department. By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement. Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers." And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress. The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage. Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls Warren and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China." Even before Democrats take control in January, Huang is expected to appear before Congress. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast , R-Fla., is actively negotiating for Huang to testify before House committees and told reporters Thursday the Nvidia CEO has agreed to appear in the coming weeks. Details of that testimony are still being worked out, Mast said. It would likely include his committee, as well as the House intelligence panel and the House Permanent Select Committee on China, and it would be under oath and transcribed. It's not clear at this point whether it would be public. "We want to see him basically in a week … Sooner rather than later," Mast told reporters Thursday, adding that he believed it would happen before Thanksgiving. If Huang doesn't willingly appear, Mast said he will subpoena him. Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., sent a second request Thursday to Huang and Teter requesting they appear and giving them an 8 p.m. ET Friday deadline to respond. Mast also sent a second request to Kessler. Rep. Josh Gottheimer , D-N.J., a member of the House Intelligence Committee, said Friday during an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" that he wants answers from Huang on the national security and export implications of the affair. "From an intelligence committee perspective, you can imagine from an AI perspective, how important this is for our national security, for our critical infrastructure and understand when it comes to chip policy, what exactly got to China and ... did Megaspeed divert chips?" Gottheimer said. The calls for immediate investigation into Huang and Nvidia on the day of his resignation represent a stunning fall from grace in the halls of power for the former CEO. Huang was one of the most effective voices for the AI industry in Washington — able to toggle between leveraging his relationship with Trump and defending his industry from fears about AI's risks to lawmakers. "He is always the TED Talk guy," one senior Democratic staff member who was granted anonymity to describe private meetings they had attended with Huang, told CNBC. "He's really good and articulate, and really good at explaining why AI is important and why it's so important for the United States to be leading here." The staffer said Huang was a "happy warrior" for AI, and stayed longer than scheduled or anticipated for questions from lawmakers. But in the meetings with lawmakers the aide attended, they said Huang did not aggressively push against export controls or get too "deep in the weeds" to really "lobby one way or the other" with the lawmakers. Huang has repeatedly resisted export controls publicly, a move that has rubbed some lawmakers the wrong way. Some lawmakers even lamented the loss of Huang, despite the inevitable buzzsaw he now faces on Capitol Hill. "It's just sad all around," Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., said of Huang's resignation. The November 23, 2026 Post article by Ian Duncan opens with a straightforward claim: for years , Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and company lobbyists pushed in Washington to protect China sales of powerful AI chips . The reporting attributes three details to two people familiar with the approach , speaking anonymously: The published excerpt also quotes Chris McGuire , identified as a former National Security Council official who helped design early Biden-era AI chip export rules , saying those rules were the product of painstaking analysis drawing on public data. Duncan’s full article continues beyond the excerpt available without a subscription; this post sticks to lines visible in the public lead and to reporting that cites the same journalists . Techmeme’s Monday digest pointed readers at Duncan’s piece alongside earlier Huang–Trump coverage. explainx.ai does not treat aggregators as sources; we use them only to notice that the November 23 URL is a new filing date , not a rewrite of the November 13 shadow-war article from Duncan, Dorfman, and Strobel. On November 20 , Duncan reported that the Commerce Department approved almost 580,000 Nvidia AI chips for China under a Trump administration plan that allowed sales in exchange for a cut of revenue . The approvals appeared in confidential documents the House Foreign Affairs Committee released. Duncan noted customers included two large Chinese tech firms the Pentagon lists as having military ties , and that the rows dated to May 2026 and do not prove chips shipped . explainx.ai mapped the same disclosure in our House Foreign Affairs license post . extraction.body: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded. Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy . But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet. Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat. "In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday. Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China . Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal. The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department. By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement. Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers." And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress. The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage. Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls Warren and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China." Even before Democrats take control in January, Huang is expected to appear before Congress. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast , R-Fla., is actively negotiating for Huang to testify before House committees and told reporters Thursday the Nvidia CEO has agreed to appear in the coming weeks. Details of that testimony are still being worked out, Mast said. passages: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded.

Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy . But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet.

Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat.

"In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday.

Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China .

Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal.

The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department.

By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement.
Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers."

And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress.
The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls

Warren and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
Even before Democrats take control in January, Huang is expected to appear before Congress.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast , R-Fla., is actively negotiating for Huang to testify before House committees and told reporters Thursday the Nvidia CEO has agreed to appear in the coming weeks.

Details of that testimony are still being worked out, Mast said. It would likely include his committee, as well as the House intelligence panel and the House Permanent Select Committee on China, and it would be under oath and transcribed. It's not clear at this point whether it would be public.
"We want to see him basically in a week … Sooner rather than later," Mast told reporters Thursday, adding that he believed it would happen before Thanksgiving.
If Huang doesn't willingly appear, Mast said he will subpoena him.

Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., sent a second request Thursday to Huang and Teter requesting they appear and giving them an 8 p.m. ET Friday deadline to respond. Mast also sent a second request to Kessler.

Rep. Josh Gottheimer , D-N.J., a member of the House Intelligence Committee, said Friday during an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" that he wants answers from Huang on the national security and export implications of the affair.

"From an intelligence committee perspective, you can imagine from an AI perspective, how important this is for our national security, for our critical infrastructure and understand when it comes to chip policy, what exactly got to China and ... did Megaspeed divert chips?" Gottheimer said.

The calls for immediate investigation into Huang and Nvidia on the day of his resignation represent a stunning fall from grace in the halls of power for the former CEO. Huang was one of the most effective voices for the AI industry in Washington — able to toggle between leveraging his relationship with Trump and defending his industry from fears about AI's risks to lawmakers.

"He is always the TED Talk guy," one senior Democratic staff member who was granted anonymity to describe private meetings they had attended with Huang, told CNBC. "He's really good and articulate, and really good at explaining why AI is important and why it's so important for the United States to be leading here."

The staffer said Huang was a "happy warrior" for AI, and stayed longer than scheduled or anticipated for questions from lawmakers. But in the meetings with lawmakers the aide attended, they said Huang did not aggressively push against export controls or get too "deep in the weeds" to really "lobby one way or the other" with the lawmakers.
Huang has repeatedly resisted export controls publicly, a move that has rubbed some lawmakers the wrong way.

"It's just sad all around," Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., said of Huang's resignation.
