The November 23, 2026 Post article by Ian Duncan opens with a straightforward claim: for years , Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and company lobbyists pushed in Washington to protect China sales of powerful AI chips . The reporting attributes three details to two people familiar with the approach , speaking anonymously: The published excerpt also quotes Chris McGuire , identified as a former National Security Council official who helped design early Biden-era AI chip export rules , saying those rules were the product of painstaking analysis drawing on public data. Duncan’s full article continues beyond the excerpt available without a subscription; this post sticks to lines visible in the public lead and to reporting that cites the same journalists . Techmeme’s Monday digest pointed readers at Duncan’s piece alongside earlier Huang–Trump coverage. explainx.ai does not treat aggregators as sources; we use them only to notice that the November 23 URL is a new filing date , not a rewrite of the November 13 shadow-war article from Duncan, Dorfman, and Strobel. Export control gate illustration for AI chip sales to China and Washington lobbying context Lobbying aims at a commercial prize. Even when Beijing blocks shipments, Commerce license math shows how large Nvidia thought that prize could be. On November 20 , Duncan reported that the Commerce Department approved almost 580,000 Nvidia AI chips for China under a Trump administration plan that allowed sales in exchange for a cut of revenue . The approvals appeared in confidential documents the House Foreign Affairs Committee released. Duncan noted customers included two large Chinese tech firms the Pentagon lists as having military ties , and that the rows dated to May 2026 and do not prove chips shipped . explainx.ai mapped the same disclosure in our House Foreign Affairs license post . The takeaway for operators: “approved” is not “delivered.” Many lines in the Mast release show Approved, not shipped , especially after Beijing import friction and Nvidia’s later decision to halt Hopper-class China shipments under interim CEO Colette Kress , covered in our Q3 FY27 earnings write-up . If you are modeling capacity, use shipped units and guidance , not license ceilings from spring 2026. CNBC writes that Huang spent roughly two years building “unparalleled” access to President Donald Trump , influencing federal AI policy while pushing looser China restrictions . CNBC attributes several verifiable or filing-backed details: CNBC also embeds a November 2026 segment titled around how Huang influenced Trump’s China policy , separate from Duncan’s November 23 print story. Treat video titles as editorial framing , not statutes. Readers searching “did lobbying win China access?” should read CNBC’s last bullet: Washington approvals did not automatically clear Chinese customs . That gap is why Bessent’s public remarks and Trump–Xi summit coverage still matter for supply planners. Executive lobbying rarely appears only in K Street filings. Huang also argued in media that curbs hurt U.S. industry . Bloomberg’s November 9 Circuit clips, documented in our export-policy post , quote Huang saying U.S. chip restrictions toward China were a mistake that is hard to unwind and that China is a competitor, not an enemy on safety dialogue. Those lines are advocacy , not Commerce regulations . The November 23 WaPo story is about mechanism — who called whom — while the Bloomberg clips are about message . Compliance teams need the EAR text and license conditions ; strategists watch both . Duncan’s November 23 deck mentions mistrust left in Washington. That theme overlaps, but does not duplicate, the Megaspeed intelligence thread . explainx.ai maintains a running claimed-vs-verified Megaspeed timeline covering board probes , Rubio memo reporting , and bipartisan briefing requests . Speaker Mike Johnson’s November 12 consensus quote shows lame-duck lawmakers still hunting NDAA language even as Huang exited the CEO role. The lobbying story explains why some officials think Nvidia had outsized influence ; the scandal story explains why others want that influence curtailed . Neither replaces reading actual export-control amendments . The November 23 Post excerpt quotes Chris McGuire in the same paragraph that introduces his biography as a former NSC staffer who helped craft the first Biden-administration limits on AI chip exports . McGuire’s public commentary after the Megaspeed reporting — including a November 2026 thread on X reproduced in CNBC’s follow-up — argued that Commerce should tighten export controls so firms linked to intelligence risks cannot keep buying frontier GPUs . That tension is the policy story behind Duncan’s “mistrust” framing: one camp treats China revenue as inevitable engagement , another treats every H-class die as a strategic asset that needs harder gates . Builders sit in the middle, executing BIS filings while executives argue on cable news. When you brief leadership, separate three layers: Only layer one is binding in court. Layers two and three explain volatility in guidance calls. This table is a reader map , not a complete chronology. Use it when someone asks “when did lobbying translate into licenses?” The honest answer is months later , and shipments lagged approvals even before Kress halted Hopper exports. sources.title: Tesla’s FSD v15 turns driving visuals into Grand Theft Auto
passages: Under the hood, FSD v15 runs on an upgraded vision encoder shared across Tesla’s FSD, Robotaxi, and Optimus humanoid robot programs.

The third-person perspective renders buildings, crosswalks, pedestrians, and surrounding traffic with a photorealism that has drawn immediate comparisons to Grand Theft Auto VI (which conveniently launched just days earlier).
By training the model on millions of online videos, Tesla claims its AI learned to prevent serious driving mistakes 25 times more often while using less computing power.

Alongside dozens of cumulative fatalities linked to Tesla’s driver-assistance systems since 2019, the probe is a stark reminder of the gap between Tesla’s autonomous ambitions and a system that still legally requires a human to keep their eyes on the road.
Tesla has begun rolling out Full Self-Driving (Supervised) v15, calling it a ground-up overhaul of its end-to-end driver assist system.
Tesla’s bold “25x” safety claim also lands amid intense federal scrutiny.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is actively investigating roughly 2.9 million FSD-equipped vehicles over reports of Teslas blowing through red lights, crossing railroad tracks improperly, and driving into oncoming lanes.
Even Elon Musk couldn’t resist the comparison on X, posting “FSD is GTA irl” shortly after the update dropped on Saturday.
Tesla also promises sharper hazard avoidance for potholes, standing water, and small animals, alongside smoother speed handling in school zones and bad weather.
For drivers who find the live feed overwhelming, Tesla includes a map-only option and a stripped-back “quiet mode”.
A new Bike Rack Mode lets drivers engage FSD even with hitch accessories attached (though it disables reversing, Summon, and Autopark).

Instead, a continuous overhead view rebuilds the street in front of the car with building windows, crosswalk stripes, parked vehicles, and pedestrians caught mid-step, all lit the way a night scene appears in a big open-world game. extraction.body: Tesla wants to make driving feel more like a video game. The latest update to its Full Self-Driving (FSD) software attempts to bring that experience to life. Tesla boss Elon Musk compared the update with the viral new video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA). But while the visuals may look like something out of a video game, the technology is dealing with real roads, real vehicles and real people.Tesla released FSD v15 to some vehicles on Saturday, November 21. Among several claimed improvements, the update introduces a feature called Tesla Reality View. And this is where things get interesting.Tesla turns the road into a video gameTesla Reality View gives drivers a photorealistic, third-person view of their car and its surroundings. Think of the camera angle in a racing game, where you can see your vehicle from behind while it moves through the world. It is a live representation of the actual road around the Tesla.According to Tesla's release notes, the feature is designed to let drivers see and understand what FSD is planning to do. Instead of looking at a relatively basic digital representation of the road, users get a more detailed view of their surroundings.Musk shared his reaction to the feature on X, writing, "It's like GTA". The comparison is easy to understand, particularly at a time when GTA VI is dominating gaming conversations. However, Tesla Reality View is not about turning driving into a game. It is meant to make the car's decisions easier to follow.Shivon Zilis, director at Neuralink, also responded to the discussion with an interesting observation: "If you zoom out a little further, you can see our simulation playing on the screen of the creators." Her comment adds another layer to the conversation around how machines represent and interpret the world around them.A video game-like view, but real-world risksThere is a reason Tesla's update is attracting attention beyond its visual appeal. Self-driving technology needs to make sense not only to the car but also to the person sitting behind the wheel. A more familiar visualisation could help drivers understand what the system is detecting and planning.But there is an important distinction here. Tesla's FSD is still a supervised driving system. The driver must remain attentive and responsible for taking control when needed. coreStoryFacts.text: Under the hood, FSD v15 runs on an upgraded vision encoder shared across Tesla’s FSD, Robotaxi, and Optimus humanoid robot programs.

The third-person perspective renders buildings, crosswalks, pedestrians, and surrounding traffic with a photorealism that has drawn immediate comparisons to Grand Theft Auto VI (which conveniently launched just days earlier).
By training the model on millions of online videos, Tesla claims its AI learned to prevent serious driving mistakes 25 times more often while using less computing power.

Alongside dozens of cumulative fatalities linked to Tesla’s driver-assistance systems since 2019, the probe is a stark reminder of the gap between Tesla’s autonomous ambitions and a system that still legally requires a human to keep their eyes on the road.
Tesla has begun rolling out Full Self-Driving (Supervised) v15, calling it a ground-up overhaul of its end-to-end driver assist system.
Tesla’s bold “25x” safety claim also lands amid intense federal scrutiny.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is actively investigating roughly 2.9 million FSD-equipped vehicles over reports of Teslas blowing through red lights, crossing railroad tracks improperly, and driving into oncoming lanes.
Even Elon Musk couldn’t resist the comparison on X, posting “FSD is GTA irl” shortly after the update dropped on Saturday.
Tesla also promises sharper hazard avoidance for potholes, standing water, and small animals, alongside smoother speed handling in school zones and bad weather.
For drivers who find the live feed overwhelming, Tesla includes a map-only option and a stripped-back “quiet mode”.

Tesla started pushing Full Self-Driving Supervised version 15 to early owners on November 21, and the screen that greets drivers once the update finishes looks nothing like the familiar gray blocks and simplified car shapes of older builds.
Tesla Reality View Adds a live visualization of the drive that lets you see & control what FSD is planning to do
Reality View brings the outside world to life by creating the scene on screen using a virtual camera looking down at the car from above.
Reality View can be displayed full screen, split so that the map takes up half the screen, or in a ‘quieter’ option to keep the journey more subdued.

Then there are the behind-the-scenes updates.

The latest software promises to operate 25 times more safely in emergency scenarios after the researchers retrained the visual recognizer on a vast collection of online movies and shared the update with the FSD, Robotaxi, and Optimus systems.
The automobile can now pick up signs, small animals, and other objects with more ease, and it adjusts its speed considerably more smoothly in school zones and severe weather.
You can now avoid speed camera slowdowns by accelerating slightly, and the car will remember to ignore any camera locations you’ve highlighted.
Bike Rack mode allows the FSD to function normally even when you have bike racks on the back, but you will still be stranded without reverse.
The driver monitoring system also works better with hats and shades on, and it is less finicky when you drive quicker.
Its turn signals are now soft, lasting only a few clicks before fading away.

extraction.body: Tesla has begun rolling out Full Self-Driving (Supervised) v15, calling it a ground-up overhaul of its end-to-end driver assist system. The centerpiece is Reality View, a real-time generative display that swaps out old wireframe graphics for a live, overhead camera angle that lets drivers see and tap to influence what the car plans to do next. The third-person perspective renders buildings, crosswalks, pedestrians, and surrounding traffic with a photorealism that has drawn immediate comparisons to Grand Theft Auto VI (which conveniently launched just days earlier). Even Elon Musk couldn’t resist the comparison on X, posting “FSD is GTA irl” shortly after the update dropped on Saturday. Under the hood, FSD v15 runs on an upgraded vision encoder shared across Tesla’s FSD, Robotaxi, and Optimus humanoid robot programs. By training the model on millions of online videos, Tesla claims its AI learned to prevent serious driving mistakes 25 times more often while using less computing power. A new Bike Rack Mode lets drivers engage FSD even with hitch accessories attached (though it disables reversing, Summon, and Autopark). The system can now automatically ease off the speed near traffic cameras, with an option to override and permanently mute specific cameras after two cancellations. Tesla also promises sharper hazard avoidance for potholes, standing water, and small animals, alongside smoother speed handling in school zones and bad weather. Meanwhile, navigation learns preferred neighborhood routes and favorite parking spots over time, and the cabin camera can now track driver attention through hats and sunglasses while dialing back nagging alerts at higher speeds. For drivers who find the live feed overwhelming, Tesla includes a map-only option and a stripped-back “quiet mode”. Tesla’s bold “25x” safety claim also lands amid intense federal scrutiny. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is actively investigating roughly 2.9 million FSD-equipped vehicles over reports of Teslas blowing through red lights, crossing railroad tracks improperly, and driving into oncoming lanes. Alongside dozens of cumulative fatalities linked to Tesla’s driver-assistance systems since 2019, the probe is a stark reminder of the gap between Tesla’s autonomous ambitions and a system that still legally requires a human to keep their eyes on the road.

passages: Tesla started pushing Full Self-Driving Supervised version 15 to early owners on November 21, and the screen that greets drivers once the update finishes looks nothing like the familiar gray blocks and simplified car shapes of older builds.
Tesla Reality View Adds a live visualization of the drive that lets you see & control what FSD is planning to do
Reality View brings the outside world to life by creating the scene on screen using a virtual camera looking down at the car from above.
Reality View can be displayed full screen, split so that the map takes up half the screen, or in a ‘quieter’ option to keep the journey more subdued.

Then there are the behind-the-scenes updates.

The latest software promises to operate 25 times more safely in emergency scenarios after the researchers retrained the visual recognizer on a vast collection of online movies and shared the update with the FSD, Robotaxi, and Optimus systems.
The automobile can now pick up signs, small animals, and other objects with more ease, and it adjusts its speed considerably more smoothly in school zones and severe weather.
You can now avoid speed camera slowdowns by accelerating slightly, and the car will remember to ignore any camera locations you’ve highlighted.
Bike Rack mode allows the FSD to function normally even when you have bike racks on the back, but you will still be stranded without reverse.
The driver monitoring system also works better with hats and shades on, and it is less finicky when you drive quicker.
Its turn signals are now soft, lasting only a few clicks before fading away.

extraction.body: Tesla started pushing Full Self-Driving Supervised version 15 to early owners on November 21, and the screen that greets drivers once the update finishes looks nothing like the familiar gray blocks and simplified car shapes of older builds. Instead, a continuous overhead view rebuilds the street in front of the car with building windows, crosswalk stripes, parked vehicles, and pedestrians caught mid-step, all lit the way a night scene appears in a big open-world game. Elon Musk watched the same footage and posted a short reply that simply read “It’s like GTA,” a comparison that stuck because the rendered world moves with the car and shows the blue path the system intends to follow. Reality View brings the outside world to life by creating the scene on screen using a virtual camera looking down at the car from above. Instead of using a pre-made graphics file, the neural engine that selects how to drive and at what speed draws that picture. As the product’s owner pointed out, this has the added benefit of requiring slightly less processing power than previously. Reality View can be displayed full screen, split so that the map takes up half the screen, or in a ‘quieter’ option to keep the journey more subdued. Coming up turns appear as little chevrons floating around in the view, and pressing on any location on the screen allows you to select a new destination or park in a specific spot, which is indicated with a small pin. extraction.body: Tesla wants to make driving feel more like a video game. The latest update to its Full Self-Driving (FSD) software attempts to bring that experience to life. Tesla boss Elon Musk compared the update with the viral new video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA). But while the visuals may look like something out of a video game, the technology is dealing with real roads, real vehicles and real people.Tesla released FSD v15 to some vehicles on Saturday, November 21. Among several claimed improvements, the update introduces a feature called Tesla Reality View. And this is where things get interesting.Tesla turns the road into a video gameTesla Reality View gives drivers a photorealistic, third-person view of their car and its surroundings. Think of the camera angle in a racing game, where you can see your vehicle from behind while it moves through the world. It is a live representation of the actual road around the Tesla.According to Tesla's release notes, the feature is designed to let drivers see and understand what FSD is planning to do. Instead of looking at a relatively basic digital representation of the road, users get a more detailed view of their surroundings.Musk shared his reaction to the feature on X, writing, "It's like GTA". The comparison is easy to understand, particularly at a time when GTA VI is dominating gaming conversations. However, Tesla Reality View is not about turning driving into a game. It is meant to make the car's decisions easier to follow.Shivon Zilis, director at Neuralink, also responded to the discussion with an interesting observation: "If you zoom out a little further, you can see our simulation playing on the screen of the creators." Her comment adds another layer to the conversation around how machines represent and interpret the world around them.A video game-like view, but real-world risksThere is a reason Tesla's update is attracting attention beyond its visual appeal. Self-driving technology needs to make sense not only to the car but also to the person sitting behind the wheel. A more familiar visualisation could help drivers understand what the system is detecting and planning.But there is an important distinction here. Tesla's FSD is still a supervised driving system. The driver must remain attentive and responsible for taking control when needed. A video game-like display does not make the car autonomous, nor does it remove the risks involved in driving.The update also brings several other claimed improvements, including better handling of potholes, school zones, speed cameras and standing water. However, as Electrek's Fred Lambert points out, FSD updates have not always improved in a straight line. New versions can bring gains in some areas while introducing problems in others.So, while Tesla's new view may make driving look a little more like GTA, the road outside the windshield is no game. And that is perhaps the most important thing for drivers to remember.- Ends

Think of the camera angle in a racing game, where you can see your vehicle from behind while it moves through the world.
It is a live representation of the actual road around the Tesla.According to Tesla's release notes, the feature is designed to let drivers see and understand what FSD is planning to do.

Instead of looking at a relatively basic digital representation of the road, users get a more detailed view of their surroundings.Musk shared his reaction to the feature on X, writing, "It's like GTA".
The comparison is easy to understand, particularly at a time when GTA VI is dominating gaming conversations.
However, Tesla Reality View is not about turning driving into a game.

It is meant to make the car's decisions easier to follow.Shivon Zilis, director at Neuralink, also responded to the discussion with an interesting observation: "If you zoom out a little further, you can see our simulation playing on the screen of the creators." Her comment adds another layer to the conversation around how machines represent and interpret the world around them.A video game-like view, but real-world risksThere is a reason Tesla's update is attracting attention beyond its visual appeal.
Self-driving technology needs to make sense not only to the car but also to the person sitting behind the wheel.
A more familiar visualisation could help drivers understand what the system is detecting and planning.But there is an important distinction here.
Tesla's FSD is still a supervised driving system.
The driver must remain attentive and responsible for taking control when needed.

A video game-like display does not make the car autonomous, nor does it remove the risks involved in driving.The update also brings several other claimed improvements, including better handling of potholes, school zones, speed cameras and standing water.
However, as Electrek's Fred Lambert points out, FSD updates have not always improved in a straight line.
New versions can bring gains in some areas while introducing problems in others.So, while Tesla's new view may make driving look a little more like GTA, the road outside the windshield is no game.
And that is perhaps the most important thing for drivers to remember.- Ends

passages: By Anhata Rooprai Nov 23 (Reuters) - CrowdStrike will acquire Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record, uniting two major players as advances in
Zscaler shares jumped more than 20% in premarket trading to $235.50, but remained well below the deal's implied value of $260.41 per share.

The deal brings together CrowdStrike's protection for computers, servers and other devices with Zscaler's technology for securing employees' access to applications and data, creating a broader cybersecurity platform for corporate and government customers.
Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share they own, implying a premium of about 34% to Zscaler's last close.
The combined company is expected to start with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue, including roughly $3.9 billion from Zscaler.
CrowdStrike expects the deal to generate about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing.
Qatalyst Partners, JPMorgan and BofA Securities are advising CrowdStrike on the transaction, while BDT & MSD Partners, Citigroup and Goldman Sachs are advising Zscaler.
Zscaler's customer base includes large companies such as Unilever and United Airlines.
CrowdStrike forecast fourth-quarter revenue of between $1.638 billion and $1.644 billion, above analysts' average estimate of $1.62 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.
It expects adjusted profit of 36 cents per share, in line with estimates.
The companies will continue to operate separately until closing.
The agreement carries a $1.4 billion breakup fee payable by Zscaler if it walks away under certain circumstances, including to accept a rival offer.
Zscaler, meanwhile, reported a 20% rise in first-quarter revenue to $949.3 million, beating estimates of $938 million.

The gap between Zscaler's trading price and the value of the offer comes as investors weigh the prospects for regulatory scrutiny of a transaction that would combine two of the cybersecurity industry's biggest players.

extraction.body: The CrowdStrike logo is displayed on the building known as Sphere, in Las Vegas, Nevada, U.S. September 1, 2026 REUTERS/Raphael Satter By Anhata Rooprai Nov 23 (Reuters) - CrowdStrike will acquire Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record, uniting two major players as advances in The CrowdStrike logo is displayed on the building known as Sphere, in Las Vegas, Nevada, U.S. September 1, 2026 REUTERS/Raphael Satter Nov 23 (Reuters) - CrowdStrike will acquire Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record, uniting two major players as advances in artificial intelligence fuel increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. The deal brings together CrowdStrike's protection for computers, servers and other devices with Zscaler's technology for securing employees' access to applications and data, creating a broader cybersecurity platform for corporate and government customers. Zscaler shares jumped more than 20% in premarket trading to $235.50, but remained well below the deal's implied value of $260.41 per share. CrowdStrike shares fell nearly 7%. The gap between Zscaler's trading price and the value of the offer comes as investors weigh the prospects for regulatory scrutiny of a transaction that would combine two of the cybersecurity industry's biggest players. "Antitrust scrutiny is certainly possible given the size of the transaction and the importance of both companies, but it would be premature to assume that regulators will necessarily try to block it," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group. "The key issue is likely to be how much overlap regulators see between the two businesses and whether customers would genuinely have fewer competitive alternatives as a result." The acquisition comes amid consolidation in the cybersecurity industry, with companies seeking to build broader platforms offering multiple services as customers look to reduce the number of security vendors they use. For CrowdStrike, the deal also opens up cross-selling opportunities by giving it access to roughly 8,000 Zscaler customers that do not currently use its products. Zscaler's customer base includes large companies such as Unilever and United Airlines. Demand for cybersecurity tools has grown as enterprises worldwide confront increasingly sophisticated attacks, with advances in AI making it easier to identify and exploit software vulnerabilities while also improving tools designed to detect and stop threats. Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share they own, implying a premium of about 34% to Zscaler's last close. CrowdStrike shareholders will own about 84% of the combined company after the transaction closes, which is expected in the second half of 2027. George Kurtz, CrowdStrike's CEO, will lead the combined company, while Zscaler chief executive Jay Chaudhry will stay on to run the Zscaler business and join CrowdStrike's board. The companies will continue to operate separately until closing. The agreement carries a $1.4 billion breakup fee payable by Zscaler if it walks away under certain circumstances, including to accept a rival offer. CrowdStrike said the deal would expand its addressable market by more than $185 billion, strengthening its position across a broader range of cybersecurity products and services. The combined company is expected to start with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue, including roughly $3.9 billion from Zscaler. CrowdStrike expects the deal to generate about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing. Qatalyst Partners, JPMorgan and BofA Securities are advising CrowdStrike on the transaction, while BDT & MSD Partners, Citigroup and Goldman Sachs are advising Zscaler. The deal was announced alongside strong quarterly results from both companies. CrowdStrike forecast fourth-quarter revenue of between $1.638 billion and $1.644 billion, above analysts' average estimate of $1.62 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. It expects adjusted profit of 36 cents per share, in line with estimates. Third-quarter revenue rose 28% to $1.58 billion, helped by a 29% increase in subscription revenue. Analysts had expected total revenue of $1.53 billion. Adjusted profit was 34 cents per share, above estimates of 31 cents. Zscaler, meanwhile, reported a 20% rise in first-quarter revenue to $949.3 million, beating estimates of $938 million. Adjusted profit of $1.23 per share also topped estimates of $1.16. passages: CrowdStrike on Monday, November 23, announced an agreement to acquire Zscaler in an all-stock transaction valued at approximately $43.9 billion, one of the largest deals in the cybersecurity industry, as companies race to strengthen defences against increasingly sophisticated cyber threats.

The acquisition brings together CrowdStrike's endpoint security capabilities and Zscaler's cloud-based network security platform, creating a broader cybersecurity offering at a time when enterprises are seeking integrated solutions to combat rapidly evolving threats.
Separately, CrowdStrike forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $1.638 billion to $1.644 billion, ahead of analysts' expectations of about $1.62 billion.

Under the terms of the agreement, Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share they own, valuing the company at $260.41 per share, a premium of about 34% to its previous closing price.
CrowdStrike said the combination would expand its total addressable market by more than $185 billion and create a business with over $10 billion in annual recurring revenue at the time of closing.
George Kurtz, chief executive of CrowdStrike, will lead the combined company.

The companies said they will continue to operate independently until the deal closes, which is expected in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

The deal comes amid growing concerns that advances in artificial intelligence are enabling cybercriminals to identify and exploit software vulnerabilities more quickly, increasing demand for tools that can detect, prevent and respond to attacks across corporate networks.

coreStoryFacts.text: CrowdStrike plans to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in an all-stock deal that combines two significant security businesses at a time when artificial intelligence is supercharging attacks.
CrowdStrike has been a major beneficiary of skyrocketing demand for AI security, with shares soaring about 80% this year as of Monday's open.
Zscaler shares are up about 5% year to date after Monday's surge.
Their combined market value exceeded $265 billion as of Friday's close, behind market leader Palo Alto Networks at $282 billion.
The deal is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal year 2028.
Under the agreement, Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share.
Shares of CrowdStrike dropped roughly 5% in early trading Monday, while Zscaler surged more than 20%.
CrowdStrike on Monday also reported better-than-expected fiscal third-quarter results , including earnings of 34 cents per share on $1.58 billion in revenue.

"With Zscaler, we're building cybersecurity's operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely," CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said in a statement.
Zscaler's fiscal first-quarter earnings , also released on Monday, likewise surpassed estimates.
By Anhata Rooprai Nov 23 (Reuters) - CrowdStrike will acquire Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record, uniting two major players as advances in
Zscaler shares jumped more than 20% in premarket trading to $235.50, but remained well below the deal's implied value of $260.41 per share.

The deal brings together CrowdStrike's protection for computers, servers and other devices with Zscaler's technology for securing employees' access to applications and data, creating a broader cybersecurity platform for corporate and government customers.
Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share they own, implying a premium of about 34% to Zscaler's last close.
The combined company is expected to start with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue, including roughly $3.9 billion from Zscaler.
CrowdStrike expects the deal to generate about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing.
Qatalyst Partners, JPMorgan and BofA Securities are advising CrowdStrike on the transaction, while BDT & MSD Partners, Citigroup and Goldman Sachs are advising Zscaler.
Zscaler's customer base includes large companies such as Unilever and United Airlines.
CrowdStrike forecast fourth-quarter revenue of between $1.638 billion and $1.644 billion, above analysts' average estimate of $1.62 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.
It expects adjusted profit of 36 cents per share, in line with estimates.
The companies will continue to operate separately until closing.
The agreement carries a $1.4 billion breakup fee payable by Zscaler if it walks away under certain circumstances, including to accept a rival offer.
Zscaler, meanwhile, reported a 20% rise in first-quarter revenue to $949.3 million, beating estimates of $938 million.

The gap between Zscaler's trading price and the value of the offer comes as investors weigh the prospects for regulatory scrutiny of a transaction that would combine two of the cybersecurity industry's biggest players.

George Kurtz, chief executive of CrowdStrike, will lead the combined company.

The companies said they will continue to operate independently until the deal closes, which is expected in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

The deal comes amid growing concerns that advances in artificial intelligence are enabling cybercriminals to identify and exploit software vulnerabilities more quickly, increasing demand for tools that can detect, prevent and respond to attacks across corporate networks.

"Antitrust scrutiny is certainly possible given the size of the transaction and the importance of both companies, but it would be premature to assume that regulators will necessarily try to block it," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group. passages: CrowdStrike on Monday, November 23, announced an agreement to acquire Zscaler in an all-stock transaction valued at approximately $43.9 billion, one of the largest deals in the cybersecurity industry, as companies race to strengthen defences against increasingly sophisticated cyber threats.

The acquisition brings together CrowdStrike's endpoint security capabilities and Zscaler's cloud-based network security platform, creating a broader cybersecurity offering at a time when enterprises are seeking integrated solutions to combat rapidly evolving threats.
Separately, CrowdStrike forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $1.638 billion to $1.644 billion, ahead of analysts' expectations of about $1.62 billion.

Under the terms of the agreement, Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share they own, valuing the company at $260.41 per share, a premium of about 34% to its previous closing price.
CrowdStrike said the combination would expand its total addressable market by more than $185 billion and create a business with over $10 billion in annual recurring revenue at the time of closing.
George Kurtz, chief executive of CrowdStrike, will lead the combined company.

The companies said they will continue to operate independently until the deal closes, which is expected in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

The deal comes amid growing concerns that advances in artificial intelligence are enabling cybercriminals to identify and exploit software vulnerabilities more quickly, increasing demand for tools that can detect, prevent and respond to attacks across corporate networks.

In a surprise move, Nvidia 's board reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO on Monday, just days after rejecting his offer to return to the artificial intelligence chipmaker where he built a reputation as one of the industry's leading evangelists.
It was the latest twist in the fallout from Huang's admission of an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board Chairman Harvey C. Jones said in a statement.

President Donald Trump, who has a close personal relationship with Huang, called for the reinstatement as recently as Sunday night and took credit for the board's decision in an interview Monday with CNBC.
"I believe my intervention was very important," Trump said.

The president said he spoke to Huang about the reinstatement Sunday, and the CEO assured him that he would work harder than before his fall. Trump also said his administration assured Nvidia there were no national security concerns about Huang's return.
"The board decided to do what we wanted them to do," the president said.
Trump declined to say whether he called into the board meeting, though he said, "Basically, I was represented at the board."

Huang still faces scrutiny, including several congressional investigations , over the affair and the suspected diversion of Nvidia's advanced chips to China. Huang is scheduled to sit for an interview next week with three House committees investigating the scandal's implications for national security.
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said the administration's rush to reinstate Huang "underscores the need for Congress to act."

"Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing" by the administration, Huang, other NVIDIA executives and "anyone selling out our national security for financial gain," Schumer said in a statement.

Huang said in a statement that he was "honored" to return to the company and that he resumes the responsibility "with the greatest humility and renewed commitment." He thanked Jones and interim CEO Colette Kress, who will return to her role as chief financial officer, as well as Nvidia's executive staff for their leadership during the brief period of disorder.

"I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support," Huang's statement said. "Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can't wait to get back to work."

Shares of Nvidia soared 33% to $165.57 at the opening bell Monday, moments after Huang's return was announced. That price was far below the all-time high of $239.24 that the stock reached just last month.
The president said Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed that the government "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

Trump called the reinstatement the "correct and proper decision," writing on social media Monday that the country "needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy." He also called for Nvidia to continue its internal investigation.

The company has had a whirlwind month after Huang admitted to extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, a suspected spy for the country. Nvidia stock was at the center of market volatility in the wake of the admission and its downstream effects in Washington.
Attorney General Blanche told reporters at an unrelated news conference this month that the Justice Department had not reached any conclusion about whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy.
"All that I think I will say is that of course DOJ is investigating or looking at it," Blanche said.

extraction.body: Delta Air Lines experienced widespread flight delays Sunday, Nov. 22, after a technical problem with its aircraft weight-and-balance automation system disrupted operations at its Atlanta hub and affected flights across the country. The disruption came just days before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel periods of the year. At the airline’s request, the Federal Aviation Administration instituted a morning ground stop for Delta and its regional carriers headed toward Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport before downgrading the measure to a ground delay program shortly after 8:40 a.m. EST. Federal aviation officials emphasized in a public statement that the disruption was strictly an internal carrier issue and “not related to any FAA air traffic systems”. The operational bottleneck stemmed from an outage in Delta’s Automated Load Instruction System, the software responsible for calculating an aircraft’s total weight and center of gravity prior to takeoff. Because pilots rely on these exact metrics to determine safe takeoff speeds and engine thrust, crew members had to compute load distributions by hand while technicians worked to bring the technology back online. “Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the company said in a statement. “We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism”. By midday, flight-tracking data from FlightAware recorded more than 1,160 delayed Delta flights nationwide—accounting for roughly a third of all U.S. air travel delays—with over 700 disruptions concentrated at the carrier’s Atlanta mega-hub. Federal regulators had projected average hold times of 57 minutes to space out arrivals and prevent tarmac congestion, though some travelers faced waits nearing two hours. Ripple effects quickly reached major East Coast and Midwest hubs, slowing departures in cities including New York, Boston, Newark, Minneapolis, and Miami, even as the FAA formally lifted the Atlanta delay program at 11:28 a.m. EST. The timing compounded frustration for fliers kicking off one of the busiest travel weeks of the year, with AAA projecting nearly 6 million Americans to fly domestically for the holiday. Sunday’s breakdown also marked the third notable U.S. aviation disruption in less than two weeks, following a nationwide FAA network failure on Nov. 13 and a 90-minute departure hold at United Airlines caused by a similar system issue last week. While Hartsfield-Jackson officials confirmed that other airlines continued operating normally, Delta cautioned that it was coordinating closely with air traffic controllers to manage gate availability as teams worked through the morning backlog. extraction.body: Delta Air Lines experienced widespread flight delays Sunday, Nov. 22, after a technical problem with its aircraft weight-and-balance automation system disrupted operations at its Atlanta hub and affected flights across the country. The disruption came just days before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel periods of the year. At the airline’s request, the Federal Aviation Administration instituted a morning ground stop for Delta and its regional carriers headed toward Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport before downgrading the measure to a ground delay program shortly after 8:40 a.m. EST. Federal aviation officials emphasized in a public statement that the disruption was strictly an internal carrier issue and “not related to any FAA air traffic systems”. The operational bottleneck stemmed from an outage in Delta’s Automated Load Instruction System, the software responsible for calculating an aircraft’s total weight and center of gravity prior to takeoff. Because pilots rely on these exact metrics to determine safe takeoff speeds and engine thrust, crew members had to compute load distributions by hand while technicians worked to bring the technology back online. “Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the company said in a statement. “We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism”. By midday, flight-tracking data from FlightAware recorded more than 1,160 delayed Delta flights nationwide—accounting for roughly a third of all U.S. air travel delays—with over 700 disruptions concentrated at the carrier’s Atlanta mega-hub. Federal regulators had projected average hold times of 57 minutes to space out arrivals and prevent tarmac congestion, though some travelers faced waits nearing two hours. Ripple effects quickly reached major East Coast and Midwest hubs, slowing departures in cities including New York, Boston, Newark, Minneapolis, and Miami, even as the FAA formally lifted the Atlanta delay program at 11:28 a.m. EST. The timing compounded frustration for fliers kicking off one of the busiest travel weeks of the year, with AAA projecting nearly 6 million Americans to fly domestically for the holiday. Sunday’s breakdown also marked the third notable U.S. aviation disruption in less than two weeks, following a nationwide FAA network failure on Nov. 13 and a 90-minute departure hold at United Airlines caused by a similar system issue last week. While Hartsfield-Jackson officials confirmed that other airlines continued operating normally, Delta cautioned that it was coordinating closely with air traffic controllers to manage gate availability as teams worked through the morning backlog. extraction.body: Q.security , a New York-based cybersecurity startup focused on post-quantum cryptography, has emerged from stealth with $11.5 million in seed funding to help enterprises prepare their security infrastructure for emerging quantum computing threats. Announced November 23, 2026, the financing was led by Castle Island Ventures, with participation from New York Life Ventures and Coinbase Ventures. Additional investors include Fin Capital, SBI US Gateway Fund, a joint investment initiative of SBI Holdings and Plug and Play, and Ground Up Ventures. Founded in 2026 by cybersecurity executives Guy Peer and Nir Steinherz , Q.security has developed an artificial intelligence-powered platform designed to help organizations identify, prioritize and remediate cryptographic vulnerabilities. The company’s technology addresses the growing need for post-quantum cryptography (PQC), which involves transitioning existing encryption systems to algorithms designed to withstand attacks from sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Q.security’s platform connects an organization’s business priorities with its cryptographic inventory, helping cybersecurity teams determine which systems and applications require attention first. The platform incorporates a conversational AI interface that allows teams to investigate potential exposures and coordinate remediation activities. It also integrates with existing enterprise security and infrastructure tools, using AI-guided procedures, automated workflows and ticketing systems to manage remediation. Following implementation, the platform verifies changes and continuously monitors an organization’s cryptographic security posture. “Enterprises know they need to prepare for Q-Day, but understanding the associated risks is just the first step,” said Matt Walsh , general partner at Castle Island Ventures. Walsh highlighted concerns surrounding harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks, in which adversaries collect encrypted information today with the intention of decrypting it when quantum computing capabilities advance. He said Q.security provides organizations with a practical approach to managing cryptographic migration, from initial assessment through remediation. The company’s founders bring experience in enterprise cryptography, financial services security and digital asset protection. Peer, Q.security’s CEO, previously co-founded Unbound Security, where he led research and development through the company’s acquisition by Coinbase in 2021. Steinherz previously served as director of product at Coinbase and vice president of Strategy and Product at Unbound Security. He also held the position of senior vice president at Citi’s Security Innovation Center, where he worked on secure digital banking initiatives supporting more than 100 million customers. According to Q.security, the founders’ experience includes leading a cryptographic migration protecting hundreds of billions of dollars in assets. “Quantum computing is making cryptographic risk an urgent and ongoing business priority,” said Peer. “Nir and I founded Q.security to give enterprises the confidence to evolve the cryptography their business depends on.” The company plans to use the seed financing to introduce its platform to enterprise customers through direct sales and channel partnerships. Its approach emphasizes continuous cryptographic management rather than treating post-quantum migration as a one-time technology upgrade. By connecting business risk assessments with technical remediation, Q.security aims to help chief information security officers allocate resources and maintain compliance as encryption standards and security requirements evolve. The launch comes as organizations increasingly evaluate their exposure to future quantum computing threats and consider how to modernize encryption across complex technology environments. Q.security develops enterprise post-quantum cryptography remediation software combining business risk assessment, AI-assisted workflows, automated validation and continuous security monitoring.

Founded by cybersecurity veterans from Coinbase and Citi, Q.security offers a business-focused AI platform that manages post-quantum cryptography remediation from initial discovery through implementation and completion.

NEW YORK, NY, Nov. 23, 2026 — Q.security , a provider of business-focused post-quantum cryptography (PQC) remediation solutions, has officially launched following its emergence from stealth with $11.5 million in seed funding. The funding round was led by Castle Island Ventures, with participation from New York Life Ventures and Coinbase Ventures. Founded by cybersecurity and cryptography veterans from Coinbase and Citi, the company aims to help enterprises manage their transition to quantum-safe cryptographic systems through an AI-powered platform that coordinates remediation from initial discovery to completion.

As quantum computing advances, organizations face increasing pressure to identify and address vulnerabilities in existing encryption systems. Q.security’s platform addresses this challenge by connecting enterprise business priorities with cryptographic inventories, applications, and infrastructure. This approach enables security teams to identify critical exposures, allocate resources effectively, and manage post-quantum migration through a coordinated remediation process.

The platform provides an integrated view of business operations and cryptographic assets, allowing organizations to assess potential risks and prioritize remediation activities. Through a conversational AI interface, security teams can investigate vulnerabilities and execute remediation tasks using AI-guided runbooks, ticketing systems, and automation. The platform also integrates with existing enterprise cybersecurity and infrastructure solutions to support the implementation and verification of security fixes. Continuous monitoring capabilities help organizations maintain their cryptographic security posture as standards and emerging threats evolve.

“Enterprises know they need to prepare for Q-Day, but understanding the associated risks is just the first step. With harvest-now, decrypt-later (HNDL) data collection already under way, the challenge is determining how to prioritize the migration across business and technology environments,” said Matt Walsh, General Partner at Castle Island Ventures. “Q.security is addressing this gap by providing security leaders with a practical path starting at assessment and ending in remediation. We believe the team’s deep expertise positions Q.security well to address one of the most significant emerging challenges in enterprise cybersecurity.”

Q.security was established by Guy Peer and Nir Steinherz, who bring extensive backgrounds in cryptography, cybersecurity, and enterprise technology. Both founders have experience leading large-scale cryptographic migration initiatives, including projects involving the protection of hundreds of billions of dollars in assets.

Guy Peer, CEO of Q.security, previously co-founded Unbound Security, where he led research and development from the company’s early product stages through its acquisition by Coinbase in 2021. Nir Steinherz has held several senior leadership positions, including Director of Product at Coinbase, Vice President of Strategy and Product at Unbound Security, and Senior Vice President at Citi’s Security Innovation Center. At Citi, he led secure digital banking initiatives focused on protecting customer identities and supporting high-volume transactions for more than 100 million customers.

“Quantum computing is making cryptographic risk an urgent and ongoing business priority,” said Guy Peer. “Nir and I founded Q.security to give enterprises the confidence to evolve the cryptography their business depends on. Our PQC remediation platform gives them lasting control over that evolution, so cryptography keeps pace with the business instead of holding it back.”

The newly secured $11.5 million in seed capital will support the company’s expansion into the enterprise market through direct sales and channel partnerships. In addition to the lead investors, Q.security has received backing from Fin Capital, SBI US Gateway Fund, a joint investment fund of SBI Holdings and Plug and Play, and Ground Up Ventures.

Q.security develops a business-first post-quantum cryptography (PQC) remediation platform designed to help enterprises transition toward quantum-safe security environments. Its platform transforms cryptographic migration into a coordinated program by connecting business risks with organizational cryptographic inventories and prioritizing remediation based on asset criticality.

The Q platform uses AI-guided workflows to support vulnerability discovery, remediation execution, validation, and continuous cryptographic posture management. By integrating with existing enterprise infrastructure, the platform enables security leaders to maintain control over cryptographic transitions and adapt to changing security threats, regulatory requirements, and industry standards.

Founded in 2026 by Guy Peer and Nir Steinherz, Q.security brings together the team behind Unbound Security, which was acquired by Coinbase in 2021. The company is supported by an advisory board of cryptography and post-quantum security experts and backed by Castle Island Ventures, New York Life Ventures, Coinbase Ventures, and other investors.

The company’s technology addresses the growing need for post-quantum cryptography (PQC), which involves transitioning existing encryption systems to algorithms designed to withstand attacks from sufficiently powerful quantum computers.
Q.security’s platform connects an organization’s business priorities with its cryptographic inventory, helping cybersecurity teams determine which systems and applications require attention first.

Founded by cybersecurity and cryptography veterans from Coinbase and Citi, the company aims to help enterprises manage their transition to quantum-safe cryptographic systems through an AI-powered platform that coordinates remediation from initial discovery to completion.
In addition to the lead investors, Q.security has received backing from Fin Capital, SBI US Gateway Fund, a joint investment fund of SBI Holdings and Plug and Play, and Ground Up Ventures.

Q.security’s platform addresses this challenge by connecting enterprise business priorities with cryptographic inventories, applications, and infrastructure.
This approach enables security teams to identify critical exposures, allocate resources effectively, and manage post-quantum migration through a coordinated remediation process.

NEW YORK, NY, Nov. 23, 2026 — Q.security , a provider of business-focused post-quantum cryptography (PQC) remediation solutions, has officially launched following its emergence from stealth with $11.5 million in seed funding. The funding round was led by Castle Island Ventures, with participation from New York Life Ventures and Coinbase Ventures. Founded by cybersecurity and cryptography veterans from Coinbase and Citi, the company aims to help enterprises manage their transition to quantum-safe cryptographic systems through an AI-powered platform that coordinates remediation from initial discovery to completion.

As quantum computing advances, organizations face increasing pressure to identify and address vulnerabilities in existing encryption systems. Q.security’s platform addresses this challenge by connecting enterprise business priorities with cryptographic inventories, applications, and infrastructure. This approach enables security teams to identify critical exposures, allocate resources effectively, and manage post-quantum migration through a coordinated remediation process.

The platform provides an integrated view of business operations and cryptographic assets, allowing organizations to assess potential risks and prioritize remediation activities. Through a conversational AI interface, security teams can investigate vulnerabilities and execute remediation tasks using AI-guided runbooks, ticketing systems, and automation. The platform also integrates with existing enterprise cybersecurity and infrastructure solutions to support the implementation and verification of security fixes. Continuous monitoring capabilities help organizations maintain their cryptographic security posture as standards and emerging threats evolve.

“Enterprises know they need to prepare for Q-Day, but understanding the associated risks is just the first step. With harvest-now, decrypt-later (HNDL) data collection already under way, the challenge is determining how to prioritize the migration across business and technology environments,” said Matt Walsh, General Partner at Castle Island Ventures. “Q.security is addressing this gap by providing security leaders with a practical path starting at assessment and ending in remediation. We believe the team’s deep expertise positions Q.security well to address one of the most significant emerging challenges in enterprise cybersecurity.”

Q.security was established by Guy Peer and Nir Steinherz, who bring extensive backgrounds in cryptography, cybersecurity, and enterprise technology. Both founders have experience leading large-scale cryptographic migration initiatives, including projects involving the protection of hundreds of billions of dollars in assets.

Guy Peer, CEO of Q.security, previously co-founded Unbound Security, where he led research and development from the company’s early product stages through its acquisition by Coinbase in 2021. Nir Steinherz has held several senior leadership positions, including Director of Product at Coinbase, Vice President of Strategy and Product at Unbound Security, and Senior Vice President at Citi’s Security Innovation Center. At Citi, he led secure digital banking initiatives focused on protecting customer identities and supporting high-volume transactions for more than 100 million customers.

“Quantum computing is making cryptographic risk an urgent and ongoing business priority,” said Guy Peer. “Nir and I founded Q.security to give enterprises the confidence to evolve the cryptography their business depends on. Our PQC remediation platform gives them lasting control over that evolution, so cryptography keeps pace with the business instead of holding it back.”

The newly secured $11.5 million in seed capital will support the company’s expansion into the enterprise market through direct sales and channel partnerships. In addition to the lead investors, Q.security has received backing from Fin Capital, SBI US Gateway Fund, a joint investment fund of SBI Holdings and Plug and Play, and Ground Up Ventures.

Q.security develops a business-first post-quantum cryptography (PQC) remediation platform designed to help enterprises transition toward quantum-safe security environments. Its platform transforms cryptographic migration into a coordinated program by connecting business risks with organizational cryptographic inventories and prioritizing remediation based on asset criticality.

The Q platform uses AI-guided workflows to support vulnerability discovery, remediation execution, validation, and continuous cryptographic posture management. By integrating with existing enterprise infrastructure, the platform enables security leaders to maintain control over cryptographic transitions and adapt to changing security threats, regulatory requirements, and industry standards.

Founded in 2026 by Guy Peer and Nir Steinherz, Q.security brings together the team behind Unbound Security, which was acquired by Coinbase in 2021. The company is supported by an advisory board of cryptography and post-quantum security experts and backed by Castle Island Ventures, New York Life Ventures, Coinbase Ventures, and other investors.

passages: Post-quantum cryptography startup Q Security Inc. formally launched today with $11.5 million in new funding for a platform designed to take enterprises from discovery through to completion of their quantum-safe migrations.

Founded this year, Q.security offers a remediation platform that runs the move to post-quantum cryptography as one coordinated program. The company argues that security teams need business context to decide which cryptographic findings to address first, since the time and resources available for the work are limited.

At the core of the Q.security offering is a map of an organization’s business structure and applications. Findings from the cryptographic inventory are tied back to that map, with the highest-risk assets put at the front of the queue.

Teams are said to be able to investigate exposure and work through remediation using a conversational artificial intelligence interface. Through integrations with existing cybersecurity and infrastructure tools, the platform drives fixes to completion using AI-guided runbooks, ticketing and automation.

Once a fix is in place, Q.security verifies that it works. Monitoring of the organization’s cryptographic posture then continues as standards and threats change, an approach the company claims lets security teams reduce risk faster and at lower cost.

“Quantum computing is making cryptographic risk an urgent and ongoing business priority,” said Guy Peer, co-founder and chief executive of Q.security, who previously co-founded Unbound Security and led its research and development through its acquisition by Coinbase Global Inc. , announced in 2021.

Peer’s co-founder, Nir Steinherz, was director of product at Coinbase and vice president of strategy and product at Unbound Security. He was also a senior vice president at Citigroup Inc.’s Security Innovation Center, where he led secure digital banking initiatives for more than 100 million customers. The pair are said to have led a cryptographic migration protecting hundreds of billions of dollars in assets.
The funding is intended to support Q.security as it brings its platform to enterprise customers through direct sales and channel partners.
Castle Island Ventures led the seed round, with New York Life Ventures, Coinbase Ventures, Fin Capital, SBI US Gateway Fund and Ground Up Ventures also participating.

Matt Walsh, general partner at Castle Island Ventures, said enterprises know they need to prepare for the day quantum computers can break current encryption. With harvest-now, decrypt-later data collection already under way, “the challenge is determining how to prioritize the migration across business and technology environments,” he added.

extraction.body: Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, has been at the centre of an alleged Chinese spy and suspected chip smuggling row ever since ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair. However, a 52-year-old Chinese national has now reportedly emerged as a key behind-the-scenes player.The United States suspected Alice Huang of being a Chinese spy, a claim that has been dismissed by Beijing. The entire row related to her and the affair with Jensen Huang led to his exit from Nvidia, triggering multiple investigations into the company's chip deals, Megaspeed and other related links.In this entire suspected spy-and-chip-smuggling scene, a new face has entered. Chinese national Li Ming, who's currently out on bail in Singapore, was a central operator of a network of companies that smuggled restricted Nvidia AI chips into China, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Among these companies was Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was a managing director. Li was reportedly involved neck-deep in Megaspeed's activities and was also a part of their major decisions. Meanwhile, he also played a key role in other companies trading Nvidia chips. The surfacing of new, previously unknown connections, such as Li Ming's, shows that the efforts to help China close the gap in the AI race went far beyond the Megaspeed row.In February 2025, Li, along with others, was charged with fraud in Singapore in connection with an alleged transhipment of Nvidia chips, according to the report. Several other companies had been named in the case, but not Megaspeed.How Li Ming routed Nvidia chips to ChinaLi allegedly purchased computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips on the pretext that the hardware was for his local firm, Luxuriate Your Life. Instead, he shipped those servers to Malaysia, from where they were later moved to an unknown third location.By the time charges were filed in Singapore, Li had been working with Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, for years, the WSJ report said. Alice and her husband then set up a cloud-computing joint venture, Century Longteng, in 2021, according to Chinese corporate registry records cited by the report.Two years later, in January 2023, Li appeared in a photo on social media showing him visiting a Shanghai AI equipment company. The post referred to Li as Century Longteng's chief strategy officer.ALSO READ | As Alice Huang pursued Nvidia chips, her husband built a $9 billion China data-center empireAt the time, the Biden administration had just curbed sales of Nvidia's semiconductors to China. However, Chinese tech companies' sudden demand for the world's best AI chips had two possible reasons. One, to legally access Nvidia computing abroad—a logistically difficult move that requires transferring large amounts of data across borders. Second, to smuggle hardware into China.Li, along with Alice Huang and Kang Wei, began setting up partners in Southeast Asia to bring advanced computing power to Chinese consumers, people familiar with the business said, according to the WSJ. They acquired a Chinese video game company's Singapore unit and renamed it Megaspeed, with Alice Huang listed as a company director.Then, Megaspeed told Nvidia that Chinese tech giant Alibaba was an anchor customer and went on to become a member of the chipmaker's cloud partner programme in November 2023. This played in Megaspeed's favour as the partner status allowed the company priority access to buy the latest chips.Megaspeed reportedly brought servers to Malaysia and provided offshore computing power to Alibaba. Some of these servers were also reportedly sent to a tech company called Century Litong in Shanghai in violation of the US export controls. An investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations was launched in 2024. In May 2025, records were requested from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed, and subsequently, in June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its internal "no-sell" list.ALSO READ | Nvidia ‘no longer’ shipping Hopper data centre AI chips to China as US tightens export curbsMeanwhile, in February 2025, Singapore also launched a probe into Megaspeed and several of its senior executives over suspected false declarations involving server purchases. In this investigation, insufficient evidence of criminal offences was found in Singapore. However, Alice Huang was given a stern warning and was barred from re-entering the country.Alice's husband, Kang Wei, was detained in Shanghai earlier this year as part of a probe into suspected stock-market manipulation, the WSJ reported.Notably, Megaspeed clarified allegations of chip smuggling and said that Alice Huang left the firm in August 2025. It also affirmed that it conducts "legitimate and lawful business."Jensen Huang's Nvidia exitJensen Huang's affairs with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, and an internal company employee, among others, cost him his 33-year-long stint at Nvidia.On November 12, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive officer. The company's board said that he stepped down as president, CEO and board member with immediate effect.Nvidia's board of directors then appointed Colette Kress, its executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO. She will continue to serve in her previous roles alongside her interim office until a permanent replacement is appointed.ALSO READ | Indian-American executive Jay Puri oversaw Nvidia chip sales to Alice Huang: ReportThe chipmaker's board also launched an internal inquiry into Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, though it has already said that it doesn't believe national security or company secrets were compromised.In view of the ongoing row, Jensen Huang also reportedly agreed to brief the US Congress next month on his affair with a suspected Chinese spy. He will appear before a joint meeting of the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select committees on December 1, Bloomberg reported, citing a statement from the panels' chairman.Jensen Huang reportedly accepted the congressional invitation under the threat of a possible subpoena from Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast and China panel chair John Moolenaar to compel him to show up.

According to a recent Wall Street Journal report, Li Ming, Alice Huang's husband and business associate, played a central role in establishing operations across Southeast Asia to provide Chinese customers with access to Nvidia-powered computing infrastructure. Beyond Li, another individual closely involved in the operations of Singapore-based Megaspeed, where Alice served as a managing director, was Kang Wei. He reportedly had a say in key business decisions and was also linked to several other companies involved in trading Nvidia chips. According to the WSJ, Li had been working with Alice Huang and Kang Wei for several years before the changes to Megaspeed's corporate structure were filed. Singapore prosecutors alleged that Li purchased computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips under the pretext that the hardware would be used by his Singapore-based company, Lucuriate Your Life. Beyond their Nvidia-related business interests, Alice Huang and Kang Wei also established a cloud-computing venture called Century Longteng, with Li later identified as its chief strategy officer. In January 2023, Li appeared in social media photographs during a visit to an artificial intelligence equipment company in Shanghai. Alice Huang and Megaspeed's links to the alleged network According to the WSJ, Li Ming, Alice Huang and Kang Wei established partnerships across Southeast Asia to help Chinese customers access Nvidia-powered computing infrastructure. Their Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, joined Nvidia's cloud partner programme in November 2023, claiming Alibaba as an anchor customer to secure priority access to the chipmaker's advanced processors. However, some Nvidia-powered servers were allegedly moved to Shanghai-based technology company Century Litong, potentially violating US export controls. Li reportedly played a significant role in Megaspeed's operations and was linked to a wider network of companies involved in trading Nvidia chips. The report also highlighted Kang Wei's expanding business interests in China's data-centre sector, adding another dimension to the network's alleged operations. While Alice Huang was reportedly involved in efforts to secure access to restricted Nvidia chips, Kang was building and expanding his business interests in China's computing infrastructure industry. Megaspeed placed on Nvidia's no-sale list Following an internal investigation, documents from the US departments of Commerce and Justice reportedly revealed details of a probe into Megaspeed over potential export-control violations. The investigation began in 2024, while records of sales to the company were sought from Nvidia in May 2025. In June 2025, Nvidia reportedly placed Megaspeed on an internal 'no-sale' list. Records also show that Singapore authorities had launched an investigation into the company in 2025. However, the investigation reportedly found insufficient evidence of criminal offences. Meanwhile, Kang Wei was detained in Shanghai earlier this year as part of a separate investigation into suspected stock market manipulation. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang also reportedly initiated an internal inquiry into Jensen Huang's alleged relationship amid suspicions of possible links to Chinese intelligence.
