extraction.body: Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, has been at the centre of an alleged Chinese spy and suspected chip-smuggling controversy ever since former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair. However, a 52-year-old Chinese national has now reportedly emerged as a key behind-the-scenes player. The United States suspected Alice Huang of being a Chinese spy, a claim dismissed by Beijing. The controversy surrounding her alleged affair with Jensen Huang led to his exit from Nvidia, triggering multiple investigations into the company's chip deals, Megaspeed and other related connections. A new figure has now emerged in the alleged spy and chip-smuggling controversy. Chinese national Li Ming, who is currently out on bail in Singapore, was a central operator of a network of companies that smuggled restricted Nvidia AI chips into China, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Among these companies was Megaspeed, where Alice Huang served as a managing director. Li was reportedly deeply involved in Megaspeed's activities and participated in major decisions. He also played a key role in other companies trading Nvidia chips. The emergence of previously unknown connections, such as Li Ming's, shows that efforts to help China close the gap in the AI race extended far beyond the Megaspeed controversy. In February 2025, Li, along with others, was charged with fraud in Singapore in connection with an alleged transhipment of Nvidia chips, according to the report. Several other companies were named in the case, but not Megaspeed. Li allegedly purchased computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips, claiming that the hardware was intended for his local firm, Luxuriate Your Life. However, prosecutors in Singapore alleged that this was a false claim. Instead, he shipped the servers to Malaysia, from where they were later moved to an unknown third location. By the time charges were filed in Singapore, Li had been working with Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, for years, the WSJ report said. Alice and her husband then established a cloud-computing joint venture, Century Longteng, in 2021, according to Chinese corporate registry records cited by the report. Two years later, in January 2023, Li appeared in a photograph shared on social media showing him visiting a Shanghai-based AI equipment company. The post identified Li as Century Longteng's chief strategy officer. At the time, the Biden administration had just restricted sales of Nvidia's semiconductors to China. However, Chinese technology companies' sudden demand for the world's leading AI chips had two possible explanations. One was to legally access Nvidia computing resources abroad, a logistically difficult process requiring large amounts of data to be transferred across borders. The second was to smuggle the hardware into China. Li, Alice Huang and Kang Wei began establishing partnerships in Southeast Asia to bring advanced computing power to Chinese consumers, people familiar with the business said, according to the WSJ. They acquired the Singapore unit of a Chinese video game company and renamed it Megaspeed, with Alice Huang listed as a company director. Megaspeed then told Nvidia that Chinese technology giant Alibaba was an anchor customer and became a member of the chipmaker's cloud partner programme in November 2023. This worked in Megaspeed's favour, as the partnership status gave the company priority access to purchase the latest chips. Megaspeed reportedly brought servers to Malaysia and provided offshore computing power to Alibaba. Some of these servers were also reportedly sent to a Shanghai-based technology company called Century Litong in violation of US export controls. Alice Huang and Kang Wei's Century Longteng was a major shareholder of Century Litong until 2024, the WSJ report said. While Alice Huang was reportedly having an extramarital affair with Jensen Huang to secure access to Nvidia's advanced computing chips, Kang was busy building a vast network of government-backed data centres across China, the WSJ had previously reported, citing a review of Chinese public records. From 2021 to 2024, proposed investments linked to Kang's network totalled more than $9 billion, all backed by the government. Although Alice Huang's pitch to Nvidia identifying Alibaba as a Megaspeed customer secured the company priority access to the chipmaker's products, her efforts were derailed in 2025 by Nvidia's internal investigation. The US Departments of Commerce and Justice recently revealed details of their investigation into Megaspeed. A probe into potential export control violations by the company was launched in 2024. In May 2025, records were requested from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. Subsequently, in June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its internal "no-sell" list. Meanwhile, Singapore launched a probe into Megaspeed and several of its senior executives in February 2025 over suspected false declarations involving server purchases. The investigation found insufficient evidence of criminal offences in Singapore. However, Alice Huang was given a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country. Alice's husband, Kang Wei, was detained in Shanghai earlier this year as part of an investigation into suspected stock market manipulation, the WSJ reported. Megaspeed has denied allegations of chip smuggling and said Alice Huang left the firm in August 2025. It also maintained that it conducts "legitimate and lawful business". Jensen Huang's alleged affairs with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, and an internal company employee, among others, cost him his 33-year-long stint at Nvidia. On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive officer. The company's board said he stepped down as president, CEO and board member with immediate effect. Nvidia's board of directors then appointed Colette Kress, its executive vice-president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO. She will continue in her previous roles alongside her interim position until a permanent replacement is appointed. The chipmaker's board also launched an internal inquiry into Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, although it has already said it does not believe national security or company secrets were compromised. In light of the ongoing controversy, Jensen Huang also reportedly agreed to brief the US Congress next month about his affair with a suspected Chinese spy. He will appear before a joint meeting of the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select committees on 1 December, Bloomberg reported, citing a statement from the panels' chairman. Jensen Huang reportedly accepted the congressional invitation under the threat of a possible subpoena from Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast and China Select Committee Chairman John Moolenaar to compel him to appear. However, a 52-year-old Chinese national has now reportedly emerged as a key behind-the-scenes player.

The United States suspected Alice Huang of being a Chinese spy, a claim dismissed by Beijing. The controversy surrounding her alleged affair with Jensen Huang led to his exit from Nvidia, triggering multiple investigations into the company's chip deals, Megaspeed and other related connections.

A new figure has now emerged in the alleged spy and chip-smuggling controversy. Chinese national Li Ming, who is currently out on bail in Singapore, was a central operator of a network of companies that smuggled restricted Nvidia AI chips into China, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Among these companies was Megaspeed, where Alice Huang served as a managing director. Li was reportedly deeply involved in Megaspeed's activities and participated in major decisions. He also played a key role in other companies trading Nvidia chips.
The emergence of previously unknown connections, such as Li Ming's, shows that efforts to help China close the gap in the AI race extended far beyond the Megaspeed controversy.

In February 2025, Li, along with others, was charged with fraud in Singapore in connection with an alleged transhipment of Nvidia chips, according to the report. Several other companies were named in the case, but not Megaspeed.

Li allegedly purchased computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips, claiming that the hardware was intended for his local firm, Luxuriate Your Life. However, prosecutors in Singapore alleged that this was a false claim. Instead, he shipped the servers to Malaysia, from where they were later moved to an unknown third location.

By the time charges were filed in Singapore, Li had been working with Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, for years, the WSJ report said. Alice and her husband then established a cloud-computing joint venture, Century Longteng, in 2021, according to Chinese corporate registry records cited by the report.

Two years later, in January 2023, Li appeared in a photograph shared on social media showing him visiting a Shanghai-based AI equipment company. The post identified Li as Century Longteng's chief strategy officer.

At the time, the Biden administration had just restricted sales of Nvidia's semiconductors to China. However, Chinese technology companies' sudden demand for the world's leading AI chips had two possible explanations. One was to legally access Nvidia computing resources abroad, a logistically difficult process requiring large amounts of data to be transferred across borders. The second was to smuggle the hardware into China.

Li, Alice Huang and Kang Wei began establishing partnerships in Southeast Asia to bring advanced computing power to Chinese consumers, people familiar with the business said, according to the WSJ. They acquired the Singapore unit of a Chinese video game company and renamed it Megaspeed, with Alice Huang listed as a company director.

Megaspeed then told Nvidia that Chinese technology giant Alibaba was an anchor customer and became a member of the chipmaker's cloud partner programme in November 2023. This worked in Megaspeed's favour, as the partnership status gave the company priority access to purchase the latest chips.

Megaspeed reportedly brought servers to Malaysia and provided offshore computing power to Alibaba. Some of these servers were also reportedly sent to a Shanghai-based technology company called Century Litong in violation of US export controls. Alice Huang and Kang Wei's Century Longteng was a major shareholder of Century Litong until 2024, the WSJ report said.

While Alice Huang was reportedly having an extramarital affair with Jensen Huang to secure access to Nvidia's advanced computing chips, Kang was busy building a vast network of government-backed data centres across China, the WSJ had previously reported, citing a review of Chinese public records.
From 2021 to 2024, proposed investments linked to Kang's network totalled more than $9 billion, all backed by the government.

Although Alice Huang's pitch to Nvidia identifying Alibaba as a Megaspeed customer secured the company priority access to the chipmaker's products, her efforts were derailed in 2025 by Nvidia's internal investigation.
The US Departments of Commerce and Justice recently revealed details of their investigation into Megaspeed. A probe into potential export control violations by the company was launched in 2024.
In May 2025, records were requested from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. Subsequently, in June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its internal "no-sell" list.

Meanwhile, Singapore launched a probe into Megaspeed and several of its senior executives in February 2025 over suspected false declarations involving server purchases. The investigation found insufficient evidence of criminal offences in Singapore. However, Alice Huang was given a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country.
Alice's husband, Kang Wei, was detained in Shanghai earlier this year as part of an investigation into suspected stock market manipulation, the WSJ reported.
Megaspeed has denied allegations of chip smuggling and said Alice Huang left the firm in August 2025. It also maintained that it conducts "legitimate and lawful business".
Jensen Huang's alleged affairs with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, and an internal company employee, among others, cost him his 33-year-long stint at Nvidia.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive officer. The company's board said he stepped down as president, CEO and board member with immediate effect.

Nvidia's board of directors then appointed Colette Kress, its executive vice-president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO. She will continue in her previous roles alongside her interim position until a permanent replacement is appointed.

The chipmaker's board also launched an internal inquiry into Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, although it has already said it does not believe national security or company secrets were compromised.
In light of the ongoing controversy, Jensen Huang also reportedly agreed to brief the US Congress next month about his affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
He will appear before a joint meeting of the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select committees on 1 December, Bloomberg reported, citing a statement from the panels' chairman.

Jensen Huang reportedly accepted the congressional invitation under the threat of a possible subpoena from Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast and China Select Committee Chairman John Moolenaar to compel him to appear.

Chinese national Li Ming, who's currently out on bail in Singapore, was a central operator of a network of companies that smuggled restricted Nvidia AI chips into China, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

They acquired a Chinese video game company's Singapore unit and renamed it Megaspeed, with Alice Huang listed as a company director.Then, Megaspeed told Nvidia that Chinese tech giant Alibaba was an anchor customer and went on to become a member of the chipmaker's cloud partner programme in November 2023.

However, Alice Huang was given a stern warning and was barred from re-entering the country.Alice's husband, Kang Wei, was detained in Shanghai earlier this year as part of a probe into suspected stock-market manipulation, the WSJ reported.Notably, Megaspeed clarified allegations of chip smuggling and said that Alice Huang left the firm in August 2025.

Alice and her husband then set up a cloud-computing joint venture, Century Longteng, in 2021, according to Chinese corporate registry records cited by the report.Two years later, in January 2023, Li appeared in a photo on social media showing him visiting a Shanghai AI equipment company.
Meanwhile, he also played a key role in other companies trading Nvidia chips.

He will appear before a joint meeting of the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select committees on December 1, Bloomberg reported, citing a statement from the panels' chairman.Jensen Huang reportedly accepted the congressional invitation under the threat of a possible subpoena from Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast and China panel chair John Moolenaar to compel him to show up.

The entire row related to her and the affair with Jensen Huang led to his exit from Nvidia, triggering multiple investigations into the company's chip deals, Megaspeed and other related links.In this entire suspected spy-and-chip-smuggling scene, a new face has entered.
However, Chinese tech companies' sudden demand for the world's best AI chips had two possible reasons.
One, to legally access Nvidia computing abroad—a logistically difficult move that requires transferring large amounts of data across borders.

Investigations into the alleged affair involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang have brought another key figure into focus in the alleged network used to divert Nvidia's artificial intelligence chips to China.

According to a recent Wall Street Journal report, Li Ming, Alice Huang's husband and business associate, played a central role in establishing operations across Southeast Asia to provide Chinese customers with access to Nvidia-powered computing infrastructure.
The report also highlighted Kang Wei's expanding business interests in China's data-centre sector, adding another dimension to the network's alleged operations.
He reportedly had a say in key business decisions and was also linked to several other companies involved in trading Nvidia chips.
Singapore prosecutors alleged that Li purchased computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips under the pretext that the hardware would be used by his Singapore-based company, Lucuriate Your Life.
Among these companies was Megaspeed, where Alice Huang served as a managing director.
Li was reportedly deeply involved in Megaspeed's activities and participated in major decisions.
He also played a key role in other companies trading Nvidia chips.

While Alice Huang was reportedly having an extramarital affair with Jensen Huang to secure access to Nvidia's advanced computing chips, Kang was busy building a vast network of government-backed data centres across China, the WSJ had previously reported, citing a review of Chinese public records.
A new figure has now emerged in the alleged spy and chip-smuggling controversy.
The United States suspected Alice Huang of being a Chinese spy, a claim dismissed by Beijing.
Alice and her husband then established a cloud-computing joint venture, Century Longteng, in 2021, according to Chinese corporate registry records cited by the report.

However, a 52-year-old Chinese national has now reportedly emerged as a key behind-the-scenes player.The United States suspected Alice Huang of being a Chinese spy, a claim that has been dismissed by Beijing. Among these companies was Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was a managing director. Li was reportedly involved neck-deep in Megaspeed's activities and was also a part of their major decisions. Meanwhile, he also played a key role in other companies trading Nvidia chips. The surfacing of new, previously unknown connections, such as Li Ming's, shows that the efforts to help China close the gap in the AI race went far beyond the Megaspeed row.In February 2025, Li, along with others, was charged with fraud in Singapore in connection with an alleged transhipment of Nvidia chips, according to the report. This played in Megaspeed's favour as the partner status allowed the company priority access to buy the latest chips.Megaspeed reportedly brought servers to Malaysia and provided offshore computing power to Alibaba. Some of these servers were also reportedly sent to a tech company called Century Litong in Shanghai in violation of the US export controls. An investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations was launched in 2024. According to a recent Wall Street Journal report, Li Ming, Alice Huang's husband and business associate, played a central role in establishing operations across Southeast Asia to provide Chinese customers with access to Nvidia-powered computing infrastructure. Beyond Li, another individual closely involved in the operations of Singapore-based Megaspeed, where Alice served as a managing director, was Kang Wei. He reportedly had a say in key business decisions and was also linked to several other companies involved in trading Nvidia chips. According to the WSJ, Li had been working with Alice Huang and Kang Wei for several years before the changes to Megaspeed's corporate structure were filed. Singapore prosecutors alleged that Li purchased computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips under the pretext that the hardware would be used by his Singapore-based company, Lucuriate Your Life. Beyond their Nvidia-related business interests, Alice Huang and Kang Wei also established a cloud-computing venture called Century Longteng, with Li later identified as its chief strategy officer. In January 2023, Li appeared in social media photographs during a visit to an artificial intelligence equipment company in Shanghai. Alice Huang and Megaspeed's links to the alleged network According to the WSJ, Li Ming, Alice Huang and Kang Wei established partnerships across Southeast Asia to help Chinese customers access Nvidia-powered computing infrastructure. Their Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, joined Nvidia's cloud partner programme in November 2023, claiming Alibaba as an anchor customer to secure priority access to the chipmaker's advanced processors. However, some Nvidia-powered servers were allegedly moved to Shanghai-based technology company Century Litong, potentially violating US export controls. Li reportedly played a significant role in Megaspeed's operations and was linked to a wider network of companies involved in trading Nvidia chips. The report also highlighted Kang Wei's expanding business interests in China's data-centre sector, adding another dimension to the network's alleged operations. While Alice Huang was reportedly involved in efforts to secure access to restricted Nvidia chips, Kang was building and expanding his business interests in China's computing infrastructure industry. Megaspeed placed on Nvidia's no-sale list Following an internal investigation, documents from the US departments of Commerce and Justice reportedly revealed details of a probe into Megaspeed over potential export-control violations. The investigation began in 2024, while records of sales to the company were sought from Nvidia in May 2025. In June 2025, Nvidia reportedly placed Megaspeed on an internal 'no-sale' list. Records also show that Singapore authorities had launched an investigation into the company in 2025. However, the investigation reportedly found insufficient evidence of criminal offences. Meanwhile, Kang Wei was detained in Shanghai earlier this year as part of a separate investigation into suspected stock market manipulation. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang also reportedly initiated an internal inquiry into Jensen Huang's alleged relationship amid suspicions of possible links to Chinese intelligence.

Senior researcher at the Al Jazeera Centre for Studies Attacks on commercial vessels appear to have become an established tactic in ongoing wars. In the Gulf region, they are part of the continuing war of attrition between the United States and Iran. In the Black Sea, they have become an increasingly prominent feature of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. Most of the vessels being targeted are not military ships but commercial ones carrying oil, gas and petroleum products, or food commodities such as wheat and corn. All are essential either to the functioning of the economy or to human survival. In October, commercial shipping in the Black Sea witnessed a sharp escalation, with a series of drone attacks targeting at least nine vessels off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, both NATO members. This is a dangerous development through which Moscow is testing the alliance’s cohesion. Several NATO members have already complained of Russian incursions into their territory, raising questions about whether Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, which provides for collective defence, could be invoked. Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukrainian ports on the Black Sea and the Danube River. With most Ukrainian ports disrupted, Kyiv has turned to alternative routes to export its grain to markets in Africa and the Middle East. These fall into three main categories: But these alternative corridors have not escaped Russian attacks. According to a report by maritime security company Ambrey , the monthly rate of attacks associated with the Danube corridor was 3.7 times higher in the July-September quarter than in the first half of 2026. Meanwhile, the Danube’s share of cargo handled at Ukrainian ports jumped from about 10 percent during January-June to 74 percent in August 2026. Seeking to inflict maximum damage and losses on each other, neither Russia nor Ukraine has shied away from using every available means to deter or subdue the other. While the war initially focused on military and logistical facilities, attacks subsequently expanded to infrastructure and ports, then gradually to refineries and energy installations. Today, food-related facilities and ships carrying grain and other food products are increasingly in the line of fire. At the beginning of the war, Moscow concentrated its strikes on Ukraine’s infrastructure for producing grain and oilseeds. It obstructed access to Ukrainian ports on the Black Sea and repeatedly targeted vessels carrying grain. This forced Ukraine to secure alternative export routes, including the Danube, which has itself become a target of Russian attacks. Grain and vegetable oil exports are a vital part of Ukraine’s economy. Data indicate that they accounted for about 40 percent of the country’s total merchandise exports in the first half of this year. This helps explain why Russia has concentrated its strikes on ports and vessels transporting these economically vital products. Ukraine’s agriculture minister estimates that if the ports remain closed, the country will lose at least $8bn between June this year and June 2027. That shortfall would be equivalent to 20 percent of its total export revenues last year. Russian attacks on cargo vessels and export infrastructure have largely brought maritime traffic through Ukraine’s Black Sea ports to a halt. These ports previously handled about 90 percent of the country’s agricultural exports. On the other side, Russian grain production and exports had, until recently, remained relatively insulated from attacks. But this summer, Kyiv redirected its drones towards Russian grain and vegetable oil export facilities, as well as commercial vessels, including grain carriers. This marked a significant shift in the economic war, as Ukrainian strikes had previously focused more heavily on Russian energy installations and military facilities. Ukrainian attacks disrupted main Russian grain export terminals on the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, forcing Moscow to divert some of its exports to Baltic Sea ports. The Sea of Azov had previously handled nearly a quarter of Russia’s wheat exports. Russia is the world’s largest wheat exporter, while Ukraine ranks fifth. Together, they account for nearly 27 percent of global wheat exports. Recent attacks have pushed wheat futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange to their highest levels since 2023, with prices rising by about 20 percent in the first nine months of this year. The escalation of attacks by both sides has coincided with the peak wheat export season in each country. Winter wheat, the dominant variety grown in Russia and Ukraine, is harvested in summer and exported in late summer and early autumn. Ukrainian attacks, particularly those targeting Russian ports on the Sea of Azov and at Novorossiysk, have reportedly knocked out an estimated 70 percent of Russia’s grain export capacity. Recent Russian attacks, meanwhile, have halted shipments from Odesa, putting nearly 90 percent of Ukrainian grain shipments out of operation. Ukraine also intensified its attacks on cargo ships departing Russian ports in July and August. According to Ukrainian military officials, they struck 76 Russian vessels between July 6 and 11. In mid-July, Russia suspended exports through the Don-Azov Canal. Russian wheat exports via the Sea of Azov suffered a further setback following a Ukrainian attack on a major grain export terminal at the Russian port of Taman in late July. As the saying goes, misfortunes rarely come alone. Attacks on food-related facilities and supply routes involving two of the world’s largest grain producers have coincided with a decline in global wheat production caused by drought and climate change. According to estimates by the US Department of Agriculture, the combined production of the world’s seven largest wheat-exporting countries is likely to fall by 11 percent in the 2026-27 season. Together, these developments pose a dual threat to global food security. The capacity to produce food is declining, while the ability to deliver it to importing markets is being disrupted, amid rising transport costs and the growing expense of securing shipments. Ultimately, the war unfolding in the Black Sea will translate into higher food prices, rising import bills and the depletion of strategic reserves, particularly in Arab and African countries that depend heavily on imported grain. The disruption of energy supplies caused by the war in Gulf waters is already fuelling inflation. Now, the decline in food supplies resulting from the war in the Black Sea threatens to add another, equally dangerous source of inflation. Attacks on commercial vessels appear to have become an established tactic in ongoing wars. In the Gulf region, they are part of the continuing war of attrition between the United States and Iran. In the Black Sea, they have become an increasingly prominent feature of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. Most of the vessels being targeted are not military ships but commercial ones carrying oil, gas and petroleum products, or food commodities such as wheat and corn. All are essential either to the functioning of the economy or to human survival.

In October, commercial shipping in the Black Sea witnessed a sharp escalation, with a series of drone attacks targeting at least nine vessels off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, both NATO members. This is a dangerous development through which Moscow is testing the alliance’s cohesion. Several NATO members have already complained of Russian incursions into their territory, raising questions about whether Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, which provides for collective defence, could be invoked.

Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukrainian ports on the Black Sea and the Danube River. With most Ukrainian ports disrupted, Kyiv has turned to alternative routes to export its grain to markets in Africa and the Middle East. These fall into three main categories:

But these alternative corridors have not escaped Russian attacks. According to a report by maritime security company Ambrey , the monthly rate of attacks associated with the Danube corridor was 3.7 times higher in the July-September quarter than in the first half of 2026. Meanwhile, the Danube’s share of cargo handled at Ukrainian ports jumped from about 10 percent during January-June to 74 percent in August 2026.

Seeking to inflict maximum damage and losses on each other, neither Russia nor Ukraine has shied away from using every available means to deter or subdue the other. While the war initially focused on military and logistical facilities, attacks subsequently expanded to infrastructure and ports, then gradually to refineries and energy installations. Today, food-related facilities and ships carrying grain and other food products are increasingly in the line of fire.

At the beginning of the war, Moscow concentrated its strikes on Ukraine’s infrastructure for producing grain and oilseeds. It obstructed access to Ukrainian ports on the Black Sea and repeatedly targeted vessels carrying grain. This forced Ukraine to secure alternative export routes, including the Danube, which has itself become a target of Russian attacks.

Grain and vegetable oil exports are a vital part of Ukraine’s economy. Data indicate that they accounted for about 40 percent of the country’s total merchandise exports in the first half of this year. This helps explain why Russia has concentrated its strikes on ports and vessels transporting these economically vital products.

Ukraine’s agriculture minister estimates that if the ports remain closed, the country will lose at least $8bn between June this year and June 2027. That shortfall would be equivalent to 20 percent of its total export revenues last year. Russian attacks on cargo vessels and export infrastructure have largely brought maritime traffic through Ukraine’s Black Sea ports to a halt. These ports previously handled about 90 percent of the country’s agricultural exports.

On the other side, Russian grain production and exports had, until recently, remained relatively insulated from attacks. But this summer, Kyiv redirected its drones towards Russian grain and vegetable oil export facilities, as well as commercial vessels, including grain carriers.

This marked a significant shift in the economic war, as Ukrainian strikes had previously focused more heavily on Russian energy installations and military facilities. Ukrainian attacks disrupted main Russian grain export terminals on the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, forcing Moscow to divert some of its exports to Baltic Sea ports. The Sea of Azov had previously handled nearly a quarter of Russia’s wheat exports.

Russia is the world’s largest wheat exporter, while Ukraine ranks fifth. Together, they account for nearly 27 percent of global wheat exports. Recent attacks have pushed wheat futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange to their highest levels since 2023, with prices rising by about 20 percent in the first nine months of this year.

The escalation of attacks by both sides has coincided with the peak wheat export season in each country. Winter wheat, the dominant variety grown in Russia and Ukraine, is harvested in summer and exported in late summer and early autumn.

Ukrainian attacks, particularly those targeting Russian ports on the Sea of Azov and at Novorossiysk, have reportedly knocked out an estimated 70 percent of Russia’s grain export capacity. Recent Russian attacks, meanwhile, have halted shipments from Odesa, putting nearly 90 percent of Ukrainian grain shipments out of operation.

Ukraine also intensified its attacks on cargo ships departing Russian ports in July and August. According to Ukrainian military officials, they struck 76 Russian vessels between July 6 and 11. In mid-July, Russia suspended exports through the Don-Azov Canal. extraction.body: Mt. Hood and wheat fields near Dufur, Oregon, November 23, 2017 (Courtesy Jim Choate) In the history of warfare, belligerents have often targeted food supplies to force opponents into submission. However, in America’s wars over the last century, threats to domestic food security have been minimal. In many ways, the United States enjoyed insulation from combat conditions overseas that could have otherwise disrupted the country’s ability to feed itself. Complacency in relative isolation from disruptive food shocks is no longer a luxury the United States can afford. We are now in an era of increased globalization, where food supply chains span the oceans. In addition, America faces the renewed rise of strategic competition as China and Russia seek to replace U.S. power across the globe. Given these new realities, timely evaluation of potential vulnerabilities to American food production is necessary. Among rising strategic competitors, Russia has explicitly demonstrated a clear willingness to target food systems. In its current war against Ukraine, the Russian military has relentlessly attacked wheat supplies and production. Yet despite the critical importance wheat plays as the foremost American dietary staple, its production is indeed vulnerable to disruption should Russia choose to act. While a full-scale conventional war with Russia is unlikely because of nuclear deterrence, the Kremlin has repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to disrupt foreign interests over the past several years, from election interference to trade wars. Targeting the U.S. wheat industry could become another preferred option for the Kremlin to wage adversarial competition at a level below the threshold of armed conflict. Given the emerging global security environment, the U.S. Government should reevaluate current policies to ensure the resilience of the wheat industry against this threat. Grain plays an enormous role in feeding the world. Approximately 47 percent of all human caloric intake today comes from grains, and the United States is a significant contributor to global grain supplies. 1 According to the United Nations (UN) Food and Agriculture Organization, the United States is the second largest grain producer in the world (behind only China), producing over 450 million metric tons, which represents 15 percent of the worldwide supply. 2 Of all grains the United States produces, Americans consume more wheat than any other, making it the country’s most essential food staple. 3 U.S. farmers raise greater volumes of corn and soybeans, but most of those commodities are used for livestock feed and biofuels. 4 Due to wheat’s central role in the American food system, consumer demand for products derived from wheat is “relatively stable and largely unaffected by changes in wheat prices or disposable income,” according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). 5 As shown in figure 1, demand for wheat in the United States continues to grow. Thus, wheat represents a worthwhile case study in evaluating U.S. resiliency to food disruption in the context of strategic competition, specifically with Russia. Some may find it hard to envision a scenario where the United States would experience wheat shortages. However, recent examples of modern countries suffering significant wheat production losses exist. Russia, the world’s largest wheat exporter, suffered extensive drought and wildfires in 2011 and lost one-third of its national wheat crop as a result. 6 China, the global leader in wheat production, suffered wheat crop losses of up to 16 percent between 2000 and 2018 due to pests and pathogens. 7 Another breadbasket of the world, Ukraine, will likely see its 2022–2023 wheat output decline by 41 percent compared to the previous year because of the Russia-Ukraine war. 8 But significant domestic concerns could pose a greater risk. In 1906, journalist Alfred Henry Lewis presciently stated, “There are only nine meals between mankind and anarchy.” Unlike any other commodity, food is the one we cannot survive without. If interruptions to the food supply occurred, the public’s confidence in future availability might begin to erode, spreading fear. Those now living below the poverty line would suffer the most, but even the broader citizenry could start losing confidence in the government’s ability to provide basic needs, fueling an already tense and polarized domestic political climate. If disruptions affected U.S. wheat production, food substitutes would play a role in softening the impact. However, given wheat’s primacy in our food system, the volume of substitutes needed could pose major challenges. A national grain reserve, similar in concept to the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, would be a logical buffer to mitigate shortages, but unfortunately, no such reserve exists. Despite producing more grain than any other country on earth, China has established a national reserve that reportedly now contains at least 2 years’ worth of grain supplies should the country need it. 11 The United States has previously tried establishing a national grain reserve, most recently with the Bill Emerson Humanitarian Trust. However, the trust sold off its commodity holdings in response to food price spikes resulting from the 2008 financial crisis and now only holds cash reserves to help pay for famine relief needs abroad. 12 Should a worst-case scenario arise where the entire annual U.S. wheat harvest failed, existing stocks would quickly evaporate if current consumption levels remained constant. In the last crop year of 2021–2022, American farmers produced 1,646 million bushels of wheat, while domestic demand (comprised of human food use, animal feed, and seed) for the year totaled 1,117 million. 13 After factoring in exports and the previous year’s residuals, the remaining stock of U.S. wheat after the previous crop year was 669 million bushels, and this is expected to decrease further next year to its lowest levels since 2007–2008 ( table 1 ). 14 Applying a “time-to-survive” analysis to the hypothetical worst-case scenario, which measures the maximum duration that supply could match demand (assuming the previous domestic demand level held constant and exports were canceled), existing domestic wheat stocks would last only about 7 months. 15 Unlike other industries, agriculture does not have the option of surging production when a crisis arises as it is constrained by annual growing seasons. The United States could not replenish its wheat stocks with domestic production until the next summer harvest season. Food shocks and price spikes resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia’s war in Ukraine have helped Washington realize our food system’s fragility. The latest National Security Strategy under President Joe Biden cites food security as one of the top five shared global challenges. It highlights global initiatives the United States is currently leading, including efforts to urge other states to commit to “keeping food and agricultural markets open, increasing fertilizer production, and investing in climate-resilient agriculture.” 16 These efforts are worthwhile, but America must ensure its increased focus on global food insecurity does not turn a blind eye to potential vulnerabilities in domestic food production that a disruptive adversary such as Russia could exploit. Over the past two decades, while the Russian Federation has enjoyed a resurgence of economic growth and global influence under Vladimir Putin’s leadership, the Kremlin has demonstrated a repeated willingness to undermine U.S. interests. The reasons for this approach are rooted in what has become characterized as the Primakov doctrine, which “posits that a unipolar world dominated by the United States is unacceptable to Russia.” 17 In operationalizing the Primakov doctrine, Russia has been conducting a hybrid war in part to “foment chaos, create distrust in U.S. institutions, and target the preexisting divisions in the country.” 18 Through these actions, Russia has earned a reputation as a perilous threat “with the goal of overturning key elements of the international order.” 19 The second component of the Russian strategy to eliminate Ukrainian wheat is destruction. Not only have battles prevented farmers in certain regions of eastern Ukraine from tending to their fields, but Russian forces have also laid waste to Ukrainian cropland by burning vast acreages across the Donetsk, Mykolaiv, and Kherson regions. Russian bombing and missile strikes have destroyed the logistical infrastructure essential to wheat production and delivery, including irrigation systems, grain elevators, and port terminals. Seeking to damage Ukraine’s ability to recover from the conflict, Russia went so far as to target Ukraine’s National Gene Bank located in Kharkiv, which served as the country’s seed bank, housing some 160,000 specimens of plant and crop seeds. 28 A third pillar of the Russian strategy undermining wheat production in Ukraine has focused on Ukraine’s ability to export its grain. In the early days of the war, the Russian naval blockade of Ukraine’s Black Sea ports strangled Ukrainian exports, cutting off essential means for Kyiv to participate in global markets. Agricultural commodities are Ukraine’s top exports, including $4.61 billion worth of wheat alone in 2020. 29 Blockading the Black Sea ports was painful for Ukraine and the many countries relying on Ukrainian wheat to feed their populations, contributing to damaging global food price spikes and inflation over the ensuing months. Not until August 2022 did Russia agree to lift the blockade, based on a tenuous agreement brokered with assistance from the UN and Turkey. Even since the initial agreement, the Kremlin has unilaterally suspended it once and has threatened not to renew the deal. 30 Ukraine’s experience during the current Russian invasion reveals the lengths to which Russia is willing to go to intentionally attack wheat production and supplies, even when that grain is a vital component of the local and global food system. Based on this precedent, the United States and its allies must be prepared to defend against the variety of tactics Moscow could employ to attack wheat production elsewhere. Secretary of State Antony Blinken participates in roundtable discussion on food security and Vision for Adapted Crops and Soils with agricultural leaders from public and private sectors, in New York City, August 4, 2023 (Department of State/Chuck Kennedy) Competition between Washington and Moscow that is centered around grain is nothing new. Following the U.S. Civil War in the 1860s, cheap American wheat flooded global markets for the first time, pushing Russian wheat exports out of Europe. The U.S.-Russian grain trade rivalry was a key factor in conditions that ultimately ushered in World War I. 31 Wheat has continued to play a major, albeit behind the scenes role in U.S.-Russian relations ever since. When Putin became president in 2000, Russia relied on imports to meet half its domestic food needs. Prioritizing food security, the Russian president has since successfully executed initiatives to boost food production, and grain has been a critical focus. By 2017, Russia had become the world’s top wheat exporter, and the Kremlin has no plans to cede its pole position. Despite unprecedented sanctions from the West as punishment for its war in Ukraine, Russia still has plenty of buyers for its wheat exports in the Middle East and Asia as it strives to outproduce and outcompete American farmers. 32 Even China began importing Russian wheat this year after previously placing a ban on it due to concerns about the presence of a crop disease (dwarf bunt fungus). 33 The Kremlin’s agriculture minister is now on a mission to increase the value of agricultural exports by 50 percent by 2024. 34 Recent global supply chain disruptions from events such as the war in Ukraine and the COVID-19 pandemic have highlighted Moscow’s privileged position in terms of food security. Russia is the world’s top exporter of not only wheat but also fertilizer. 35 Given its relative strength in this area and a demonstrated willingness to attack Ukrainian wheat, attacking the domestic American wheat industry could become a viable option in Russia’s arsenal of hybrid warfare tactics against U.S. interests. Specific strategies Russia could employ to target U.S. wheat production can be organized into four categories of attack: The following sections will explore each of these options in depth. Among the cyber-security industry, many consider Russia to be the most capable and stealthiest of America’s cyber adversaries. In addition to the notable intrusions mentioned earlier, suspected Russian adversary groups have earned their reputation for several reasons, including developing sophisticated malware that employed novel command and control techniques, exhibiting rapid breakout times, and leading the way in targeting cloud infrastructure. 36 Cyber attacks crippling the food industry are not unprecedented. For example, suspected criminals successfully compromised the network of JBS S.A., a global meat processing company, hampering livestock slaughter operations and causing wholesale meat prices to spike. 37 Should the Kremlin set its sights on disrupting the U.S. wheat industry via cyber means, a likely approach would be targeting the infrastructure used for grain transport and storage, specifically the grain storage elevators throughout wheat production regions. These facilities comprise an essential component of the Nation’s food system, which the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has identified as 1 of the 16 sectors of critical infrastructure. 38 Farming cooperatives operating grain elevators increasingly leverage automation technologies to handle loading and unloading functions. If an adversary gained remote access to the industrial control system (ICS) network environment, they could shut down operations, preventing grain transportation to trade markets and food processors. Russian state-sponsored adversaries are known to have successfully targeted a critical infrastructure ICS environment, causing kinetic effects. A cyber unit within the Russian military was responsible for the attack on the Ukrainian power grid, resulting in nearly a quarter-million Ukrainians losing power for about 6 hours. 39 A similar attack chain methodology could disrupt control systems for other sectors of critical infrastructure, such as grain storage facilities. The three primary fertilizer nutrients required to grow crops are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Nitrogen fertilizer is derived from the Haber-Bosch process, which uses natural gas for fuel to extract nitrogen from the air to form ammonia. Phosphorus fertilizer comes from mining of nonrenewable phosphate rock. Potassium fertilizer is derived from mining nonrenewable potash. As of 2021, the United States imported 12 percent of its nitrogen, 9 percent of its phosphate, and 93 percent of its potash. 47 While America imports these materials from many friendly states, some come from less-trusted trading partners. This is especially true of potash. Russia and its close ally, Belarus, combine to provide 12 percent of America’s potassium requirements and more than 15 percent of total U.S. fertilizer imports ( figure 2). 48 Should Russia choose to disrupt wheat production by stopping potash exports, America would need to find ways to ramp up domestic mining and production or close the gap by increasing imports from friendly trade partners such as Canada, which already supplies 83 percent of potash used in the United States. A more significant cause for concern is that Russia is the world’s largest fertilizer exporter when considering all fertilizer components and is responsible for over 15 percent of total global fertilizer exports. 49 Leveraging that influence, Russia could attempt to manipulate availability on the global market, resulting in worldwide price shocks that would cascade to American consumers and place additional pressure on poorer countries already suffering from food security challenges. Russian impacts on global fertilizer trade have already contributed to financial instability. Fertilizer prices tripled after the beginning of the war in Ukraine because Russia limited exports. These limits included restrictions on exports of natural gas, which, as noted, is a crucial component for producing nitrogen fertilizer. 50 Russia also shut down an ammonia fertilizer pipeline from its Volga region to a Black Sea port to further restrict global supplies. 51 The USDA characterized the situation as “Putin’s price hike on farmers.” 52 These events contributed to soaring food costs, leading to the highest inflation rates in the United States in four decades. 53 In late 2022, the UN warned that if fertilizer prices were not reduced, the world would face a “future crisis” of food availability. UN officials have since worked to convince Russia to increase fertilizer output. 54 Thanks to rebounding global fertilizer production, fertilizer price fears have dampened for the near term. 55 Nevertheless, the situation demonstrates how the Kremlin can leverage its fertilizer superiority to harm the interests of not only the United States but also the world. Unfortunately, fertilizer availability is not the only way Moscow can flex its muscle in undermining American wheat production. Undercutting U.S. grain exports is another area where the American wheat industry is vulnerable to Russian meddling. Complicating the issue is that prior incidents of contaminated U.S. wheat exports could strengthen Russian hoax claims. The Soviet Union and several other countries complained of dirty, rotting, and insect-ridden U.S. grain in the 1980s. 62 In the mid-1990s, the USDA had to institute a regulatory program to certify wheat shipments were free of fungal disease after a Karnal bunt outbreak in the United States. 63 Recent research suggests that the Environmental Protection Agency scientific integrity and transparency failures related to pesticide use have eroded global trust and are undermining U.S. agricultural exports. 64 If Russia succeeds in taking global wheat export markets from the United States, American farmers will undoubtedly be threatened. With less market access and increasing input costs, the incentive for growing the preeminent American staple crop would dwindle, resulting in lower output and production capacity. Such an outcome, combined with other disruptive options identified in this essay, could accelerate Russian aims of undermining U.S. global power. Another vector for attacking U.S. wheat production, and one carrying potentially the broadest impact, would be a Russian attack involving pests or pathogens designed to damage crops. Such an attack would likely be done covertly to provide plausible deniability. Before the Biological and Toxin Weapons Convention of 1972 (BWC), several countries, including the United States, developed and maintained offensive biological weapons research programs. Intentional infestations targeting agriculture for nefarious purposes are not without precedent. Analysts strongly suspect manmade causes behind a debilitating outbreak of the fungus Moniliophthor perniciosa , also known as witches’ broom disease, among cocoa fields of Bahia, Brazil, beginning in 1989. 89 Potentially motivated by the perpetrator’s desire to destroy the chocolate industry to punish its wealthy landowners, the suspected attack nearly exterminated the area’s cocoa plantations over the following decade. By 2001, “Brazil went from being the world’s third-leading cocoa producer to being the 13 th .” 90 Given this potential for covert bioterrorism to exact large economic costs to a country’s agricultural industry, Russia could consider it as an increasingly attractive option as strategic competition with the United States escalates. Risk is a function of likelihood and consequence and can be mathematically described as Risk = Likelihood of an Event x Consequence (loss due to the event). 91 To aid in measuring likelihood and consequence of the four attack strategies Russia could employ to target U.S. wheat production, an expert survey was conducted. Data was collected from 30 participants in the United States who are professionals with expertise in fields related to the wheat industry, including farming, academia, information technology, and global trade. Due to the potential security concerns of identifying the experts in the survey, it was decided that all participants would remain anonymous. The survey asked each participant to assess the likelihood and consequences of the four Russian disruption scenarios: cyber attacks targeting grain infrastructure, restricting fertilizer exports, undercutting U.S. wheat exports, and agricultural bioterrorism. 92 Participants assessed the likelihood of each scenario using a 5-point Likert scale converted to the following percentages to enable calculations ( table 2 ). Participants assessed consequence using the following 5-point Likert scale based on expected economic losses ranging from less than $1 million to more than $20 billion ( table 3 ). Survey results for likelihood and consequence are captured in figure s 3 and 4 and risk scores are presented in figure 5. Calculated mean scores for likelihood and consequence for each attack scenario are found in table 4 . Further refinement of the results was conducted to ultimately generate a more robust measurement of overall risk for each scenario. To calculate an overall likelihood percentage, the sum of response percentage values (as shown in table 2) was divided by the total available percentage of all responses. To calculate the dollar value associated with the overall consequence score, the mean score for each scenario was assessed as a percentile within the associated dollar range (as shown in table 3). Funding is another limiting factor and will be necessary to incentivize American farmers to widely adopt the use of cover crops. Sustainable agriculture receives little government funding compared to industrial agriculture. The most recent Farm Bill (a package of legislation Congress passes every 5 years to support U.S. agriculture) provided less than 7 percent of its funding for conservation practices. 104 USDA can increase funding for cover crop implementation by reducing Farm Bill spending in other areas overdue for adjustment, like conventional corn subsidies. 105 USDA: Establish a National Strategic Grain Reserve. As previously noted, if Russia succeeded in some capacity to disrupt U.S. wheat production, resulting in domestic grain shortages, no current national wheat reserve exists to reduce the ensuing effects. Given how essential grain is to the U.S. food supply and the increasing probability of climate change’s impact on global grain production, a strategic grain reserve makes sense. The need for a reserve has risen in recent times. For instance, droughts in 2012 affected corn production to such an extent that the United States had to import corn from Brazil, a surprising development for America as the world’s leading corn producer. 106 Converting any remaining funds within the Bill Emerson Humanitarian Trust into a physical grain reserve and supplementing it by redirecting funding from conventional commodity crop subsidies could provide this much-needed resilience in our national food security.
