extraction.body: The bitcoin price surged to above $64,000 on Monday morning, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, as Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive and sent stocks sharply higher. Bitcoin is up about $8,500 from its weekend low of roughly $55,100, which came at about 1:17 a.m. ET on Saturday. Nvidia’s board voted unanimously to bring Huang back as president, CEO and director, effective immediately, the company said Monday morning. The board said it spoke with Huang and received input from “senior levels of the United States government,” concluding that his return “poses no national security risk.” Huang resigned on Nov. 11 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. CFO Colette Kress took over as interim CEO. The board has said an investigation into the reported foreign intelligence effort will continue, and Huang said he supports it. Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said the board believes Huang “is the right person to lead” the company. Huang called it an honor to return and said he “can’t wait to get back to work.” The company also formed a national security and export control committee and is searching for a chief compliance officer. The stock had lost nearly half its value during a seven-week losing streak, even after Nvidia reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Nov. 17. Investors worried about life without Huang, and bitcoin traded in step with the rout in technology shares. Nvidia (NVDA) shares were up roughly 31% to near $165 in premarket trading. Shares had tumbled 14% on Friday, closing out that seventh straight weekly decline, after a report that the SEC is examining the company’s accounting. Nasdaq-100 futures were up about 6.6% and S&P 500 futures about 4.2% at 9:21 a.m. ET. Bitcoin-linked equities rallied with the chipmaker. Coinbase (COIN) was up about 9% to near $111 in premarket trading, and Strategy (MSTR) gained about 16% to near $90.50. Miners with AI data center businesses led the move, with IREN up about 27%, MARA up about 16%, Riot Platforms (RIOT) up about 14% and Core Scientific (CORZ) up about 17%. Strategy also disclosed in an 8-K that it bought 457 bitcoin last week at an average of about $64,898, lifting its total to 851,305 BTC. The company’s average cost is about $75,446 per coin, so its stack is still under water at current prices. The rally follows a brutal stretch. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28% on Friday, and the S&P 500 lost 8.61% for the week while the Nasdaq dropped 10.02%. Bitcoin slid with stocks and finished last week down about 6%, its seventh straight red weekly candle. Spot bitcoin ETFs shed about $1.79 billion last week, their fourth straight week of net outflows, including roughly $669 million on Friday. Lyn Alden captured the gloom on Saturday, posting that “Bitcoin is dead right now. It fell 56%,” before telling followers to check back in two to three years. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also warned the Fed on Sunday that it may be making a “policy mistake” if it overtightens. The central bank’s next decision is Dec. 9, and a quarter-point hike is still the base case. The relief has limits. Nvidia still faces the internal investigation and the SEC inquiry, and the Fed meeting is still ahead. A reversal in chip stocks could quickly pull bitcoin lower again. Bitcoin remains nearly 50% below its October 2025 peak above $126,000, and traders will watch whether the Nvidia relief rally holds once regular trading opens. At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $63,700. Watch live, catch up on episodes, and get exclusive content on the go. extraction.body: Nearly 92% of the $404 million liquidated across crypto markets in one hour came from bearish bets caught by the sudden reversal. Bitcoin jumped more than 4% in an hour to $64,427 after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday. The sudden rally triggered $424 million in crypto market liquidations within an hour, according to CoinGlass , as traders betting on further declines were caught by the price reversal. CoinGlass rolling one-hour snapshot supplied November 23, 2026. Liquidated position values, not traders' realized net losses. Longs and shorts sum to $424.95 million; shorts account for about 88.7%. Screenshot capture time is not displayed. Later live dashboard readings can differ. Source: CoinGlass liquidation dashboard, supplied November 23, 2026 one-hour screenshot Short positions accounted for $376 million, or 92.2% of the liquidations, while bullish traders lost $31.58 million. Bitcoin led the losses with $188 million in liquidations, 95.6% of which came from short positions. Ethereum followed with around $80 million, with shorts accounting for 92.9%. Twelve categories with fully readable names and amounts in the supplied CoinGlass one-hour heatmap. Smaller and truncated tiles are excluded; these bars do not sum to the $424.95 million market total. Source: CoinGlass liquidation dashboard, supplied November 23, 2026 one-hour screenshot Together, the two largest cryptocurrencies accounted for nearly 64% of the $403.98 million liquidated during the hour. The concentration of short liquidations suggests that forced position closures amplified Bitcoin's initial rally, accelerating its recovery from last week's selloff. That decline had briefly pushed Bitcoin below $60,000 following Huang's abrupt departure from Nvidia on Nov. 12, which triggered turmoil across technology stocks and added pressure to an already struggling crypto market. Monday's reversal also lifted Nvidia shares by roughly 33% to around $170 in premarket trading, reversing part of the losses accumulated during the leadership crisis. Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang marks a dramatic reversal from its position last week, when board Chairman Harvey Jones ruled out bringing the company's co-founder back as chief executive. The board voted Monday unanimously to restore Huang as president, CEO, and a director after discussions that satisfied members about his candor and ability to lead the company. Nvidia also said senior US government officials provided input during the deliberations, giving directors confidence that Huang's return posed no national security risk. Huang's return followed mounting pressure from shareholders, technology executives and President Donald Trump, who had publicly supported reinstating the Nvidia co-founder . Strive CEO Matt Cole welcomed the decision, saying Nvidia was the largest single holding among Strive Asset Management's clients, with nearly $100 million invested through its ETFs. Cole said Strive had prepared to submit a shareholder proposal requesting an advisory vote on Huang's reinstatement before Monday's market opening, but the board acted before the proposal became necessary. Huang, who had previously expressed willingness to return, said he was honored to resume leadership of the company. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will return to her previous responsibilities. However, Huang's reinstatement does not end the investigation into reports that he was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Nvidia said its independent board committee would complete that investigation while a newly established national security and export control committee oversees trade compliance and related risks. The company is also recruiting a chief compliance officer and will continue cooperating with government investigations. Meanwhile, Bitcoin's rapid recovery marks its second sharp Nvidia-linked rally within a week. The cryptocurrency briefly reached approximately $64,600 following Nvidia's stronger-than-expected earnings last week, only to surrender most of those gains within 35 minutes. extraction.body: The bitcoin price surged to above $64,000 on Monday morning, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, as Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive and sent stocks sharply higher. Bitcoin is up about $8,500 from its weekend low of roughly $55,100, which came at about 1:17 a.m. ET on Saturday. Nvidia’s board voted unanimously to bring Huang back as president, CEO and director, effective immediately, the company said Monday morning. The board said it spoke with Huang and received input from “senior levels of the United States government,” concluding that his return “poses no national security risk.” Huang resigned on Nov. 11 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. CFO Colette Kress took over as interim CEO. The board has said an investigation into the reported foreign intelligence effort will continue, and Huang said he supports it. Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said the board believes Huang “is the right person to lead” the company. Huang called it an honor to return and said he “can’t wait to get back to work.” The company also formed a national security and export control committee and is searching for a chief compliance officer. The stock had lost nearly half its value during a seven-week losing streak, even after Nvidia reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Nov. 17. Investors worried about life without Huang, and bitcoin traded in step with the rout in technology shares. Nvidia (NVDA) shares were up roughly 31% to near $165 in premarket trading. Shares had tumbled 14% on Friday, closing out that seventh straight weekly decline, after a report that the SEC is examining the company’s accounting. Nasdaq-100 futures were up about 6.6% and S&P 500 futures about 4.2% at 9:21 a.m. ET. Bitcoin-linked equities rallied with the chipmaker. Coinbase (COIN) was up about 9% to near $111 in premarket trading, and Strategy (MSTR) gained about 16% to near $90.50. Miners with AI data center businesses led the move, with IREN up about 27%, MARA up about 16%, Riot Platforms (RIOT) up about 14% and Core Scientific (CORZ) up about 17%. Strategy also disclosed in an 8-K that it bought 457 bitcoin last week at an average of about $64,898, lifting its total to 851,305 BTC. The company’s average cost is about $75,446 per coin, so its stack is still under water at current prices. The rally follows a brutal stretch. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28% on Friday, and the S&P 500 lost 8.61% for the week while the Nasdaq dropped 10.02%. Bitcoin slid with stocks and finished last week down about 6%, its seventh straight red weekly candle. Spot bitcoin ETFs shed about $1.79 billion last week, their fourth straight week of net outflows, including roughly $669 million on Friday. Lyn Alden captured the gloom on Saturday, posting that “Bitcoin is dead right now. It fell 56%,” before telling followers to check back in two to three years. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also warned the Fed on Sunday that it may be making a “policy mistake” if it overtightens. The central bank’s next decision is Dec. 9, and a quarter-point hike is still the base case. The relief has limits. Nvidia still faces the internal investigation and the SEC inquiry, and the Fed meeting is still ahead. A reversal in chip stocks could quickly pull bitcoin lower again. Bitcoin remains nearly 50% below its October 2025 peak above $126,000, and traders will watch whether the Nvidia relief rally holds once regular trading opens. At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $63,700. Watch live, catch up on episodes, and get exclusive content on the go. The authority, whose recent statement falls just short of an outright ban, said that use of the internet-enabled and always-on glasses to record people in public is "almost always prohibited." Critics have dubbed these smart wearables as "pervert glasses" for their propensity to be used to video people without their permission, particularly to harass women. While some glasses have warning lights when users are recording, privacy advocates have argued that these alerts are not clear enough. Some people have even made phone apps capable of detecting nearby smart glasses wearers. The Dutch data protection authority warned that the glasses also produce wrong results and unsafe results. In one test carried out by the Dutch authority, a pair of unnamed glasses "gave dating advice to an adult who indicated that they are interested in a minor." The glasses also incorrectly read a medicine label and claimed to have called an ambulance when it had not. The Dutch government's advice follows a similar move by the Norwegian government , which in September said it was considering a ban on camera-enabled devices. extraction.body: Nothing is preparing to unveil its first AI-native device on December 8, with new teaser images revealing a compact, screenless gadget that could function as an AI-powered voice recorder and personal assistant. The British technology company, led by CEO Carl Pei, has confirmed the launch date but remains tight-lipped about the product’s name, capabilities and pricing. Recent images show a small device with a brushed metal finish, a large button labelled “Talk” and a second button featuring a recording symbol. Red and green LED indicators are also visible, suggesting the device could be designed to capture conversations, record notes and process spoken information using artificial intelligence. Nothing has promoted the upcoming product with the tagline “Be present. It’s noted”, adding to speculation that it will focus on AI-assisted note-taking and productivity. Pei has previously argued that one of the biggest problems facing current AI technology is what he describes as the “context gap”. While AI models are becoming increasingly sophisticated, he believes they lack sufficient information about users’ daily activities, conversations and interactions. For example, an idea discussed during a casual meeting or coffee break may never reach an AI assistant because it was not captured digitally. Nothing’s upcoming device appears designed to address this limitation by providing a dedicated way to record and potentially organise information throughout the day. Unlike rival companies developing AI-powered glasses, pendants and wearable pins, Nothing is positioning its first AI product as a productivity device rather than a potential smartphone replacement. Pei has also suggested that productivity applications will be among the first areas where dedicated AI hardware delivers meaningful benefits. The Nothing CEO has confirmed that the product will have “no new screen” and said its functionality could not simply have been delivered through a smartphone application. However, the company has not revealed whether the device will operate independently, connect to a smartphone or rely on cloud-based AI processing. Questions also remain about battery life, storage, privacy features and whether recorded conversations will be processed locally or uploaded to external servers. Nothing has confirmed that the device will begin shipping in December, although specific release dates and Australian availability have yet to be announced. The December 8 unveiling will provide the first detailed look at Nothing’s plans to expand beyond smartphones and audio products into dedicated AI hardware. passages: Four University of Chicago PhD students have joined the Polsky Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation as Polsky Science and Technology Associates, working with its technology and business development teams to support many aspects of the technology commercialization process.
She is curious about the pipeline from early-stage academic technologies to commercialization and thrilled to be part of this process.

extraction.body: Four University of Chicago PhD students have joined the Polsky Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation as Polsky Science and Technology Associates, working with its technology and business development teams to support many aspects of the technology commercialization process. The Polsky Science and Technology Associates Program provides graduate students with hands-on experience in technology commercialization. Associates screen new invention disclosures for potential intellectual property (IP) protection and analyze the commercial landscape, helping assess opportunities to move University discoveries toward practical applications. Selected through a competitive application process, the Associates gain experience with the scientific, legal, and business aspects of technology management during the yearlong program. Their work can include reviewing technologies for patentability, researching markets, identifying potential industry partners, and developing materials to support licensing. // Alexandra Ware is a PhD candidate in the Committee on Molecular Metabolism. In the Macleod Lab, she studies cancer cachexia, a debilitating effect of cancer that causes involuntary weight loss and skeletal muscle wasting. She is investigating tumor-muscle crosstalk to find biomarkers to help diagnose cancer earlier. Ware is excited to assess the innovative new technologies coming out of the University and conduct prior art searches. She is eager to translate that analysis into commercial strategy, learning to read a technology’s value through the combined lenses of science, law, and market demand, a perspective that rarely develops within traditional graduate training. // Idongesit Ekpo is a PhD candidate in biochemistry in the laboratory of Erin Adams. She investigates immune responses to Mycobacterium tuberculosis , the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. Her work focuses on MR1, a protein that presents molecular signals to T cells, and the T cells that recognize those signals. Ekpo is eager to engage with technologies within and beyond her field and to learn what makes certain technologies patentable. She is curious about the pipeline from early-stage academic technologies to commercialization and thrilled to be part of this process. // Asha Bozicevich is a PhD candidate in the Committee on Immunology, working in the laboratories of Erin Adams and Alex Muir. She studies how tumor metabolism alters antigen presentation and recognition by T cells, examining how the way tumors process nutrients affects the molecular signals these immune cells recognize. Bozicevich is excited to learn about the wide range of science happening across the University, connect with researchers from different fields, and see how promising discoveries can move beyond the lab toward real-world applications // Aditi Aryal is a PhD candidate in the Committee on Immunology. In the Concepcion Lab, she studies how AE2, a membrane protein that regulates cellular acidity, can affect T cell function and alterations in its expression can cause primary biliary cholangitis, an autoimmune disease that damages the liver’s bile ducts. Aryal is excited to learn about the wide range of scientific discoveries that happen at UChicago and to understand how decisions are made to turn a discovery into a product. She’s particularly excited to develop an acumen about patentability and intellectual property in the therapeutic space.

Many of our programs and accelerators have launched successful companies that make an impact within their industries. As our startups continue to see success, it further validates the work we are doing at the Polsky Center and grows our reputation in the startup scene. We are deeply tied into the Chicago tech, science, and startup spaces. We hold a number of strategic partnerships with similar entities in the Chicago-land area, as well as collaborate with Labs like Argonne National Laboratory and Fermilab to enhance our ability to support science ventures. The Polsky Exchange also makes a big impact on Chicago’s startup scene. It is a startup incubator featuring work and meeting spaces, a Small Business Development Center, and a full calendar of programming and workshops designed to help entrepreneurs launch and grow their ventures. Membership is composed of business owners and innovators in the community as well as UChicago students, faculty, and staff actively working on entrepreneurial ventures or involved in Polsky Center programs.

The Polsky Center also offers many hands-on learning opportunities aimed at helping students, researchers, faculty, and community members pursue their own entrepreneurial endeavors; furthermore, Polsky also offers resources to help individuals explore their interests in industries including but not limited to private equity, venture capital, entrepreneurship through acquisition, and social entrepreneurship.

Interested individuals can get involved through the Polsky Exchange . Operated by the Polsky Center, the Polsky Exchange is a startup incubator featuring work and meeting spaces, a Small Business Development Center, and a full calendar of programming and workshops designed to help entrepreneurs launch and grow their ventures. All upcoming events are featured on our website. Interested individuals can also sign up for our newsletters , which provide relevant news and also provide reminders for upcoming events, programs, and deadlines.

We hope after reading you have a better understanding of what the Polsky Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation is and how it can be of benefit to those who are interested in entrepreneurship, innovation, and investing. For more information about resources available at Chicago Booth, the student experience at Booth, and upcoming events with Admissions, please sign up to receive more information from us below. Associates screen new invention disclosures for potential intellectual property (IP) protection and analyze the commercial landscape, helping assess opportunities to move University discoveries toward practical applications. Selected through a competitive application process, the Associates gain experience with the scientific, legal, and business aspects of technology management during the yearlong program. Their work can include reviewing technologies for patentability, researching markets, identifying potential industry partners, and developing materials to support licensing. // Alexandra Ware is a PhD candidate in the Committee on Molecular Metabolism. In the Macleod Lab, she studies cancer cachexia, a debilitating effect of cancer that causes involuntary weight loss and skeletal muscle wasting. She is investigating tumor-muscle crosstalk to find biomarkers to help diagnose cancer earlier. Ware is excited to assess the innovative new technologies coming out of the University and conduct prior art searches. She is eager to translate that analysis into commercial strategy, learning to read a technology’s value through the combined lenses of science, law, and market demand, a perspective that rarely develops within traditional graduate training. // Idongesit Ekpo is a PhD candidate in biochemistry in the laboratory of Erin Adams. She investigates immune responses to Mycobacterium tuberculosis , the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. Her work focuses on MR1, a protein that presents molecular signals to T cells, and the T cells that recognize those signals. Ekpo is eager to engage with technologies within and beyond her field and to learn what makes certain technologies patentable. She is curious about the pipeline from early-stage academic technologies to commercialization and thrilled to be part of this process. // Asha Bozicevich is a PhD candidate in the Committee on Immunology, working in the laboratories of Erin Adams and Alex Muir. She studies how tumor metabolism alters antigen presentation and recognition by T cells, examining how the way tumors process nutrients affects the molecular signals these immune cells recognize. Bozicevich is excited to learn about the wide range of science happening across the University, connect with researchers from different fields, and see how promising discoveries can move beyond the lab toward real-world applications // Aditi Aryal is a PhD candidate in the Committee on Immunology. In the Concepcion Lab, she studies how AE2, a membrane protein that regulates cellular acidity, can affect T cell function and alterations in its expression can cause primary biliary cholangitis, an autoimmune disease that damages the liver’s bile ducts. Aryal is excited to learn about the wide range of scientific discoveries that happen at UChicago and to understand how decisions are made to turn a discovery into a product. She’s particularly excited to develop an acumen about patentability and intellectual property in the therapeutic space.
